title: Live: Cowboys suffer huge finals blow, Dragons face Eels
text:
North Queensland Cowboys star Reuben Cotter will miss week one of the NRL finals after being charged for a high tackle against the Raiders.

The Maroons forward was handed a grade two careless high tackle charge for his contact on Josh Papali'i in the first hit up of the match.

The Dragons and Eels look to end their seasons on a high before Penrith can wrap up the NRL minor premiership if they beat Wests Tigers by more than two points.

title: Like 'the Spirits': Hobart council slams new 'unfit for purpose' planning portal
text:
The Tasmanian government has suffered a $6.5 million cost blowout on its signature PlanBuild program, a new planning portal that was meant to speed up development approvals but has turned into a debacle.

PlanBuild was intended to be rolled out statewide.

Hobart City Council was the first to adopt the system when it went live in 2024, but the council says its implementation has frustrated council staff, residents and industry alike.

PlanBuild was designed as a uniform statewide planning scheme that would cover Tasmania's 29 councils. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

On Monday, the council unanimously backed a motion expressing its concern.

The motion described PlanBuild as "unfit for purpose", and called for an indefinite waiver of the annual $83,000 in fees paid to the Department of Justice — which runs the program — until the system is fixed.

Hobart councillor Louise Elliott, who introduced the motion and has been campaigning on the issue of planning costs and delays, described PlanBuild as "lose, lose, lose".

Louise Elliott says she has "genuine concerns" about the scheme. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

"Everyone's losing. [Hobart City Council] lose because it's a system that we have and people quite rightly think that it's our system, so we bear the heat and the reputational impact of that," she said.

" The taxpayers lose because we've now spent [more than] $12 million and 10 years on a system that is making people pull their hair out, and the community loses because it's another deterrent and another barrier to housing. "

The motion was supported by the council administration, who conceded the program's launch had been "very difficult for officers and applicants".

Hobart City Council passed a motion at Monday's meeting that called PlanBuild "unfit for purpose". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Scheme 'not up to scratch'

PlanBuild was conceived more than a decade ago, when former premier Peter Gutwein was treasurer and planning minister.

Mr Gutwein had pushed for a uniform statewide planning scheme to cover Tasmania's 29 councils. The idea was to roll out a streamlined, easy-to-use online portal for all building, plumbing and development applications, replacing the paper-based system.

PlanBuild was intended to be rolled out statewide. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Work started in the 2016-17 financial year, with a budget of $9.7 million — including $6.4 million in Commonwealth Small Business Regulatory Reform Agenda funding — after external tenders were called for by the Consumer, Building and Occupational Services (CBOS) arm of the Justice Department.

According to Benjamin Price, executive director of the Tasmanian branch of the Housing Industry Association, there was strong support at the outset.

"We were big backers of PlanBuild when it was initially brought to industry's attention," Mr Price said.

" We're still wedded to the PlanBuild promise: something that will make it simpler, easier, quicker to manage applications right across the state. "

Benjamin Price says the scheme is not working as intended. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Unfortunately, the trial has not gone well.

"Our members right across Tasmania and particularly here in the south have been saying that PlanBuild is not up to scratch," Mr Price said.

"It's not working as intended and it's not making their lives easier, [and it] isn't delivering the efficiencies that the Tasmanian government had promised.

" What we've seen is a clunky product that isn't delivering benefits to industry and isn't delivering benefits in the Hobart community. "

Maree Ashworth, client liaison officer for Hobart-based builders Ronald Young + Co Builders, deals with the PlanBuild system daily, and said she finds it incredibly frustrating.

Marie Ashworth says Ronald Young + Co Builders tries to avoid using the PlanBuild portal. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Ashworth told the ABC that for builds within the City of Hobart, her company hands the documentation over to somebody else to lodge through PlanBuild.

"We would rather put the projects to a planner, than use the system," she said.

That preference means added costs on all sides.

Mr Price echoed her concerns.

"We hear feedback from members who are architects, designers, builders and plumbers that the PlanBuild portal is too difficult to use," he said.

"We even hear from some members that they are charging more to do work in the City of Hobart area."

Escalating costs

Last year the Justice Department waived the fee for 2025-26 in recognition that the system was not working, after a similar motion by Cr Elliott was passed by Hobart City Council.

In May, the department agreed to a PlanBuild remediation project plan. The plan, obtained by the ABC, aimed to address the council's concerns by February 2027 and lay the foundation for a statewide rollout.

In June, CBOS executive director Robyn Pearce told a parliamentary estimates committee hearing: "We're working with City of Hobart to ensure that some of the user functionality issues that are being addressed are put into place [and] we'll then be looking to roll it out to further councils."

The scheme's rollout has blown out by millions. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

She conceded the PlanBuild budget had increased from the original $9.7 million to $12.8 million.

The $3.1 million difference was attributed mainly to delays with the rollout, which led to a loss of expected revenue from other councils due to take up the scheme.

Additionally, only $3 million of the expected $6.4 million in Commonwealth funding was received, with the final $3.4 million withheld due to the expiry of the original grant.

That blowout has left the state's taxpayers $6.5 million worse off, as the original expected state outlay of $3.3 million has now risen to $9.8 million — a three-fold increase.

Hobart City Council is worried that it has faced "reputational damage" during the scheme's trial. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

In correspondence with Cr Elliott, a spokesperson for the Justice Department said the total spending to date was just more than $11.6 million, of which some $3.45 million had been paid to the external developer.

"Rollout of the system to further councils remains on hold while post-implementation system enhancements are completed," the departmental spokesperson said.

"The final cost of statewide implementation cannot be determined at this point."

Cr Elliott told the ABC that despite the remediation work underway, "I do have genuine concerns that even with that extra work and the extra time and the extra money that it absorbs that we still won't end up with a product that's fit for purpose".

'Sold a pup', council says

At Monday's meeting, Cr John Kelly told the council that PlanBuild was a "disgrace".

"We have been sold a pup. We've got to toughen up here and really put our foot down with state government," he said.

"I note that we are a little bit of a laughing stock out there, not only among the building industry [but] also other councils.

"Other councils in Tasmania … don't want to touch this with a 40-foot barge pole. That is how bad this is."

John Kelly was light on praise for the scheme. (ABC News: Jano Gibson )

Hobart councillor Ryan Posselt told the meeting the PlanBuild experience was comparable with the epic Spirit of Tasmania debacle.

"[It's] kind of analogous to the Spirits," Cr Posselt said.

"We are bearing the reputational damage, frankly. We also desperately need homes constructed in the city and commercial buildings constructed in the city."

The ABC understands PlanBuild has experienced a heavy turnover of staff within CBOS amid budget cuts and a hiring freeze at the Justice Department.

The Minister for Justice, Corrections and Rehabilitation, Guy Barnett, told the ABC he was aware of concerns with PlanBuild, and that an additional $2 million had been committed in the recent state budget to "deliver a pathway forward".

"I have asked my Department to work with City of Hobart as a high priority to correct bugs in the system," he said.

"I understand that we are seeing some important improvements to the functionality, but work is ongoing.

"We'll continue to work closely with the local government sector to pursue opportunities to have development applications and permits processed faster."

title: Ex-Eagle says 'conservative and vanilla' AFL club's main focus is money
text:
Former West Coast midfielder Sharrod Wellingham says the Eagles have become "conservative and vanilla", with a focus on money rather than on-field success, following another poor AFL season.

West Coast finished 16th with four wins in 2026, which took their total victories to 15 since the beginning of the 2022 campaign.

"I feel like West Coast have become so complacent because they've got a lot of off-field success as a business and they've got a lot of things that they're doing right when it comes to making money," Wellingham said on 102.5 ABC Perth's SportsTalk program.

"I feel like that's where their focus is.

" They're not aggressive, they're not ruthless and the invisible board is definitely a factor. "

Wellingham, who was part of Collingwood's 2010 premiership side under Mick Malthouse before joining the Eagles in 2013, warned West Coast was in danger of going down the same path as other historically successful clubs that have drifted into irrelevance.

"There's the potential for West Coast to develop into an Essendon," he said.

Wellingham played 79 games for West Coast after winning a premiership with Collingwood. (Paul Kane, file photo: Getty Images)

West Coast has made several high profile changes in recent years, with the appointment of Don Pyke as chief executive, Andrew McQualter as coach, and Elizabeth Gaines as chair of the board.

But Wellingham said he didn't feel like much had changed at the club, which had struggled on the field in recent years.

He pointed to the decision to trade away pick three in 2024 to secure the services of now co-captain Liam Baker from Richmond, a decision which ultimately cost the Eagles access to the AFL Rising Star Jagga Smith.

If the Eagles had decided to draft Smith, they would have a midfield boasting Harley Reid, Elijah Hewett, Willem Duursma and Smith.

Jagga Smith was drafted by Carlton. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"It was a terrible decision," Wellingham said.

"There is zero swag that comes out of West Coast ... they're conservative and vanilla.

"I don't know where the change is going to come from. Yes, you want to have good people and be of sound culture, but you've got to have some ruthlessness.

"I feel like there's nothing that sounds like that and feels like that that's coming from the footy club at the moment."

Eagles CEO Don Pyke hinted at the club's determination to return to the AFL summit during West Coast's end of season awards, when he said "September is for finals, not functions".

title: Flights in Indonesia suspended due to volcano Mount Anak Krakatau eruption
text:
Indonesia's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has suspended flight operations for several hours due to volcanic ash from the ongoing eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau, Jakarta's main airport has posted on Instagram.

The suspension, extending a halt to 9:30am local time (12:30pm AEST) that had been scheduled until 5:30am, has affected 209 flights, including several international flights, Indonesia's Transportation Ministry said.

Anak Krakatau has been erupting since late on Friday, with volcanic ash detected in the airport early on Sunday, the ministry said in a statement.

Anak Krakatau volcano also erupted in December 2018. (Reuters: Antara Foto, Bisnis Indonesia, Nurul Hidayat)

Dispersal of volcanic ash has disrupted activities in Lampung province in Indonesia's Sumatra island and Banten province on Java, said Berton Panjaitan, a spokesperson for Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency, Badan Nasional Penanggulangan Bencana (BNPB).

"BNPB urges the public to remain calm while increasing vigilance," he said.

"In the event of ashfall, people are advised to wear masks and eye protection, reduce outdoor activities, cover water sources and exercise caution when driving, as volcanic ash can reduce visibility."

Several schools cancelled activities on Saturday, with students and residents suffering eye irritation from the ash, while fishermen cancelled their fishing trips due to the eruption, local media outlet Kompas reported.

The disaster mitigation agency said on Saturday there was no imminent risk of tsunami from the volcano.

Reuters

title: Aussie Patterson claims Diamond League Final title with 'insane' win
text:
Australia's Eleanor Patterson has continued her outstanding season by winning the women's high jump at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Patterson was joined on the podium by fellow Australian and reigning world champion, Nicola Olyslagers, who finished third.

The result gave Australia two victories across the weekend at the King Baudouin Stadium, following Cameron Myers's triumph in the men's 1,500m on the opening night.

Myers wins Diamond League Final Cameron Myers has beaten a star-studded field at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Patterson successfully cleared 2.01 metres with her final attempt at the height, edging out Ukrainian Olympic champion and world-record holder, Yaroslava Mahuchikh (1.99m).

Mahuchikh failed with her three attempts at 2.01m.

Olyslagers cleared 1.95m to round out the top-three placings.

Patterson attempted 2.03m, which is the same height as Mahuchikh's 2026 world lead, but could not manage a successful clearance.

She added the Diamond League Final title to her second Commonwealth Games gold, which she won in Glasgow in late July.

Her win came a week after she equalled her personal best (PB) of 2.02m in Germany.

"It's amazing," Patterson said.

"I've only won a Diamond League meet once before in 2023, so to win the final is insane. I knew I was in good shape after jumping 2.02m a few days ago.

"It was chilly, but I just went out to have fun and I'm super happy with how today turned out."

Eleanor Patterson celebrates her win in Brussels. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton)

Patterson said ignoring the performances of her rivals was the key to victory.

"Today, I stayed clinical and stuck to my own process, which really paid off," she said.

Australia's Olympic silver medallist Jessica Hull was third in the women's 1,500m, producing a season-best time of 3:54.73.

"It's nice to run the fastest I have all year in September, I think that shows my training works when you want to peak this time of the year," Hull said.

Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska saluted with a world-leading time and meet record of 3:54.05, which was also a PB.

Kenyan Dorcus Ewoi was second in a PB of 3:54.73, while Hull's Australian teammate Abbey Caldwell (3:57.19) finished seventh.

Meanwhile, Australia's Sarah Billings was fifth in the women's 800m with a time of 1.59.99.

Swiss star Audrey Werro claimed the meet record in winning with 1:54.75.

title: Sweeny exits US Open to end Australia's singles chances
text:
Dane Sweeny's gallant US Open campaign has come to a frustrating end with a tough third-round loss to 21st-seeded Italian Luciano Darderi.

Sweeny complained of a hip injury during a 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 defeat to the world number 22 that left Australia without a second-week singles hope in New York for the first time in five years.

Alex de Minaur's shock second-round loss to Botic van de Zandschulp meant Sweeny was Australia's last player standing at Flushing Meadows.

"It's been an amazing week, a career-changing week, but I can't help but feel a bit disappointed just with today's performance," Sweeny said.

"I just wasn't really feeling it, just not really feeling the timing and the rhythm as I have been. I just made a lot of cheap errors and that was quite frustrating.

"I was OK to lose a match, but I really wanted to test him more and bring a good level so I could make an absolute fight out of it.

"Win or lose, I wanted to really make him work for the victory at least and I wasn't able to do that."

The world number 123 only gained a last-minute entry to the US Open after two late withdrawals allowed Tennis Australia to grant Sweeny the reciprocal wildcard it initially handed to Alexei Popyrin.

Dane Sweeny reached the last 32 for the first time at a major. (Getty images/USTA: Dustin Satloff)

Despite his disappointment, Sweeny cashed in on his good fortune.

The 25-year-old turned his first US Open main-draw appearance into a watershed run to the last 32 of a major for the first time.

The Queenslander will walk away with a life-changing cheque for $402,500 and a fresh career-high ranking.

"The financial side of things, that will help with coaching and people you travel with," Sweeny said.

Sweeny is provisionally slated to climb to number 109 in the world.

If he can crack the top 100 by season's end, Sweeny will earn direct entry to the Australian Open for the first time.

"That's exciting too. But that will take care of itself," Sweeny said.

"It's hard not to worry about that because we're indoctrinated to want that low number next to our name, but I can just focus on working hard, focus on improving.

"Particularly just staying really kind to myself and trying to enjoy the journey."

American tilt takes a hit

Past US Open finalists Taylor Fritz, Madison Keys and Amanda Anisimova all crashed out in the third round, dealing a stinging blow to home fans.

Men's ninth seed ​Fritz had yet to drop a set in New York and looked well on his way to another routine victory before Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo found his best tennis to flip the script and win 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4.

It was the earliest exit in four years for the 2024 runner-up, as Cerundolo reached the ​fourth round for the first time.

The American ‌women fared no better as China's Zheng Qinwen fought back from a 5-0 deficit in the decider to beat 2017 runner-up Keys 1-6, 7-6 (7/3), 7-5, collapsing on the court in utter joy as she fights back from a career slump.

Zheng Qinwen celebrates her win over Madison Keys. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng will next face 2022 champion and former world number one, Iga Świątek, who got past Czech Marie Bouzková 7-6 (7/3), 7-6 (7/3).

Tenth-seeded Anisimova, last ​year's runner-up, was unable to reverse ‌her fortunes in a frustrating year at the majors, with a 6-2, 7-5 defeat by Anastasia Potapova.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open winner, provided the lone bright spot for the Americans when she beat Spain's Cristina Bucșa 6-3, 6-4 in the third round.

AAP/Reuters

title: Old working dogs refuse to be put out to pasture
text:
Kingsley Vaux's family has been farming at Ongerup, about 400 kilometres south-east of Perth, for more than a century.

By their side are about eight generations of working dogs, with 15-year-old Cassie the last in the line.

"They're normally gone at 10 or 12, but she still seems reasonably healthy although she's gone deaf so we're down to signals," Mr Vaux said.

"It's a bit of a fight to get her to change direction or anything, but she's teaching the young ones a little bit too, so it's still a joy to be working with her."

A seasoned professional

The border collie-huntaway cross may be deaf and arthritic, but her love for sheep work remains strong.

"[She] always wants to do work even though she's hardly capable of it these days, at 15," Mr Vaux said.

"All these jobs she's done before and she knows where they're going."

She is one of many old farm dogs who, far from being put out to pasture, remain "totally faithful" to their masters.

"You can see it in their eyes," Mr Vaux said.

" It's just devotion, isn't it? "

Manners maketh dog

Thirteen-year-old Bundy "loves getting out and amongst it", according to owner Renae Parsons, who relies on working dogs to muster thousands of sheep at her farm in Tenterden, about 330km south-east of Perth.

Bundy as a puppy. (Supplied: Renae Parsons)

The "naturally gifted" kelpie can't do as much as he used to but is still treasured by Ms Parsons.

"He's definitely one in a million," she said.

"If I could find another one like him, I'd grab it in an instant."

On one occasion, in the middle of moving 3,000 sheep, a quick-witted Bundy noticed 300 were missing and nipped off to bring back the laggards on his own.

Renae Parsons says 13-year-old kelpie Bundy is naturally gifted. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

But as much as Bundy likes work, there is one thing he won't stand for.

"He doesn't like to be yelled at," Ms Parsons said.

"You can talk firmly, but as soon as you get grumpy, he will go and sit on the ute and won't work.

"So you have to calm down and then he'll come back and start working again."

Better bond, better working dog

Jenny Parsons, who trains and breeds dogs on her Tenterden farm, says this level of care is typical of farming folk, despite their tough reputation.

"A lot of people think that farmers are rough and heartless, but when you look around at all the old dogs that they've still got and absolutely adore … you can tell that most farmers are very, very soft underneath," she said.

Jenny Parsons with her young dog, Sherlock, says the bond between a dog and trainer is crucial. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

In fact, it's this bond that makes for a great working dog.

"They have to want to work for you," she said.

" The better the bond … the bigger the try. "

Special bond

Mr Vaux is emotional walking through the graveyard on his property where each dog has an epithet.

Beth was a talker, Fudge a prankster, Quarter always knew her left from right, and Speckles loved the water.

"It's bloody hard when you leave one, when one leaves you," he said.

"They tug at the heartstrings, even now."

He knows Cassie will end up there one day soon, but for now he's grateful for his "loyal friend".

"She's a good mate, a good friend, and a good worker," he said.

"It's bloody amazing when you can hardly just move a finger and they know what you want to do."

Kingsley Vaux describes his working dog Cassie as a good mate and a good worker. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

title: Labor commits $550m for freeway upgrade in Melbourne's outer west
text:
Traffic congestion in Melbourne's outer west is the target of Labor's latest commitment ahead of the state election, with a pledge to spend $550 million upgrading the Western Freeway.

The funds to improve the section of freeway between the fast-growing areas of Melton and Caroline Springs are in addition to $1 billion promised by the Commonwealth government ahead of the 2025 election.

Under the plan, interchanges at Ferris Road, Leakes Road and Hopkins Road would be upgraded, alongside a new half interchange at Mount Cottrell Road giving local traffic direct access on and off the freeway.

"I said as a new premier my first task is to listen to what Victorians' needs are," Premier Ben Carroll said.

"They told me very clearly they wanted a relentless focus on the basics and there was nothing more important than getting our road infrastructure right and making sure hard-working Victorians can spend less time in traffic and get to spend more time with their families."

Premier Ben Carroll says the freeway funding pledge is part of a "relentless focus on the basics". (ABC News)

As part of the upgrade, the freeway will widened to three lanes in each direction between Ferris Road and Hopkins Road, and four lanes in each direction between Hopkins Road and Ballarat Road.

Once the upgrade is complete, the speed limit will be 100 km/h all the way along the Western Freeway between Ferris Road and Ballarat Road.

Mr Carroll said planning for the project was already underway with the federal money, and the promise represented Victoria "coming to the table as well".

Major Melton roads 'not suitable' for traffic conditions

As the November state election approaches, Melton City Council has been advocating for new train stations and major road upgrades to help alleviate pressure on existing railway stations and the busy section of freeway.

Upgrading the Western Freeway is among a suite of road infrastructure improvements the council has been calling for as the area's population increases by 6.61 per cent per annum — more than triple the Melbourne average of 2 per cent.

In documents outlining its advocacy on the issue, the council has stated that "major arterial roads in the City of Melton are not suitable for the existing high volume of traffic".

"They are predominantly of a rural standard with unsealed shoulders, no public lighting, open drains and non-existent bike and pedestrian paths."

The Western Freeway is used by tens of thousands of commuters each day.

Coalition's $10k healthcare worker incentives

Meanwhile, the Liberal-National Coalition has unveiled a fresh election promise aimed at bolstering healthcare workforces in country Victoria.

Under the Victorian Rural Health Workforce Incentive Scheme, which would cost $40 million over four years, doctors, nurses, dentists, midwives and other allied health professionals would be offered incentives of up to $10,000 to help fill positions in regional and rural areas.

The scheme would provide an initial payment of up to $10,000, with incentives of a similar amount offered each year the healthcare workers remains in the position.

The model is based on one which has already been operating in New South Wales.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson says those living in regional Victoria deserve access to experienced healthcare professionals. (ABC News)

Opposition leader Jess Wilson said regional Victorians deserved access to healthcare professionals with "much-needed experience".

"They deserve to access healthcare close to home," she said.

"So while we will be investing in health infrastructure right across this state ... we will actually make sure that we can attract the workforce to these destinations because you can only deliver quality healthcare in quality facilities if you have a strong healthcare workforce to do so."

The opposition has also pledged to incorporate accommodation for healthcare workers into new regional hospital developments, such as the West Gippsland Hospital and the Mildura Base Public Hospital.

title: Negotiations over 'Australia's biggest shortcut' near an end
text:
Years of complex negotiations with multiple traditional owner groups and environmental studies appear to be nearing an end, paving the way for the long-awaited sealing of the outback highway dubbed "Australia's biggest shortcut".

The Outback Way stretches 2,719 kilometres through central Australia — from Laverton in Western Australia's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland.

More than $1.2 billion has been committed to sealing the remote route by 2032.

The ongoing negotiations mean roadworks were put on hold four years ago on WA's side of the border, which stretches 736km from Laverton to the Northern Territory.

The Outback Way in WA begins at Laverton with the Great Central Road. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Road progress at 'glacial pace'

The delays prompted WA Liberal MP Rick Wilson to criticise the WA government in federal parliament in June for moving at a "glacial pace".

"There are stretches of this road that do not fall within any native title claims, and still no progress has been made. It's bureaucracy," he said.

WA Liberal MP Rick Wilson's electorate of O'Connor includes the WA stretch of the Outback Way. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

A spokesperson for WA Transport Minister Rita Saffioti defended the approach.

"Ensuring all approvals and registered ILUAs are in place will ensure the long-term success of the project, which has a key focus on delivering training, employment and economic opportunities for local and Aboriginal people and businesses," the statement said.

The WA section of the Outback Way stretches 736km along the Great Central Road. (Supplied: Goldfields-Esperance Development Council)

Remote communities support road

In this remote part of WA, known as the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, three main groups represent the people of the Yilka, Nangaanya-ku and Yarnangu.

This week, Main Roads did not say how advanced its discussions were with traditional land owner groups, only that they were continuing.

Ngaanyatjarra Council major projects advisor Ralph Addis described the Outback Way as "nationally significant" with "complex opportunities and challenges".

"We're hearing early next year [for construction] … we think the earliest works can start, the better for all concerned," he said.

Outback Highway Development Council chairman Pat Hill, who is also Shire of Laverton president, echoed those sentiments.

Pat Hill has been chairman of the Outback Highway Development Council since 1997. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"The communities out there have all had input, negotiating with Main Roads and the state government," he said.

"From what I've heard it will be starting just after Christmas … the sooner the better, obviously."

Studies reveal next phase

New documents show Main Roads has completed a clearing assessment and biological survey to seal a 171km section of the road.

Under the plan, 660 hectares of native vegetation would be cleared.

The assessments did not identify any significant impacts to threatened flora or fauna.

The reports now form part of a formal planning and approvals process Main Roads has begun alongside the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation.

The Outback Way stretches 2,719km from Laverton in WA's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland. (Supplied)

A social impact assessment by the Goldfields-Esperance Development Commission has also been completed, which questions if infrastructure along the route can support an influx of travellers.

It also raises the question of how to preserve culturally significant sites, with the loss of the current permitting system once it becomes a public road.

Other concerns include an increased risk of communicable disease, access to non-Opal fuel undermining petrol sniffing prevention and increased police enforcement.

Goldfields-Esperance Development Commission chief executive Kris Starcevich (left) after the completion of a social impact assessment for the Outback Way project. (Supplied: Facebook/Ngaanyatjarra Council Group)

Protecting places of significance

The Great Central Road currently averages 30-60 vehicles a day, but traffic volumes are estimated to increase 300 per cent over a decade once it is sealed, including a significant rise in heavy vehicle movements.

Yilka Talintji Aboriginal Corporation chairman Harvey Murray whose traditional lands cover the 171km Main Roads has surveyed said the agreement satisfied concerns about culturally significant sites, which he said would be signposted as restricted.

"We finished four, five years ago (negotiating the ILUA) and agreed on some compensation … we've been working on heritage and archaeological surveys," he said.

"They (Main Roads) keep saying next year, next year to finalise it.

"I know the Shire of Laverton have been looking at us, but it's with the state, it's quite frustrating."

Mr Murray said he has been asking for the gravel airstrip at Cosmos Newberry Aboriginal community on Yilka land to be upgraded to an all-weather airstrip.

"We're going to have a lot of accidents so we need that with lights for the RFDS (Royal Flying Doctor Service) to be able to fly 24-hours a day in emergencies," he said.

Mr Addis said the biggest concern for traditional land owners along the route remained the protection of culturally significant sites.

There are concerns about visitor behaviour involving photography and social media, including the photography of people, places or culturally sensitive features without consent.

The Outback Way cuts through some of the most remote parts of Australia. (ABC)

"People are concerned about making sure the extra volume of people coming through the lands is both supported and properly managed so people can enjoy the experience but not damage the local environment and cultural places," Mr Addis said.

title: Hawkesbury's Helping Hands charity marks 15 years of service
text:
Single mother Linda Strickland was at home in Sydney's north-west with her eight-year-old daughter one night when she heard someone getting into the bins in her backyard.

Her daughter Cassidy asked why someone was desperate enough to go through their bins to find food.

"How do I explain to her that we allow, we can let people be that hungry?" Ms Strickland said.

" I had blinkers on. I had no idea that people were that hungry. "

Hawkesbury's Helping Hands started out with Cassidy and her mother Linda making meals at home for people experiencing homelessness in the park. (Supplied: Linda Strickland)

The Windsor pair decided they had to do something about it. Linda and Cassidy made some meals, put them in plastic containers, and went to the local park where they knew people experiencing homelessness were staying.

That night, 15 years ago, Linda and Cassidy co-founded the charity Hawkesbury's Helping Hands (or HHH), which has since grown from those warm meals at the park into a warehouse that provides hampers and basic essentials for hundreds across Sydney's most disaster-prone region.

The charity handles up to 30 pallets a day during busy times, which are either Christmas or a major disaster. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Helping where disaster is no stranger

The mum-and-daughter team has since become the face of disaster response in the Hawkesbury, which in recent years has battled through more than its fair share of major events, including the 79-day Gospers Mountain bushfire in 2019–20 and five major floods between 2020 and 2022.

They have received two visits from prime ministers, by Scott Morrison in March 2022 and once by Anthony Albanese in July 2022 when the area was hit three times in the same year.

Ms Strickland remembered being called up in the middle of the night when the first flood hit in February 2020 off the back of the Black Summer bushfires. She said years of being a service with connections in the community meant they were ready to step up.

Scott Morrison visited HHH while he was prime minister when flooding hit the Hawkesbury in March 2022. (ABC News)

"I was called in the middle of the night to set up an evacuation centre because, being a homelessness service, we had air mattresses, we had pet supplies, we had snacks," Ms Strickland said.

"We were already prepared."

" Now we are prepared even better because five floods has taught us a lot. "

Outside of major natural disasters, the charity of around 20 volunteers has been a lifeline for the community during droughts, the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing cost-of-living crisis.

High in the warehouse, air mattresses and sleeping bags are pre-wrapped for the next major disaster. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

At their busiest, which was usually around Christmas when some other charities were not operating, Ms Strickland said they were moving between 20 and 30 pallets of food a day, which is donated by food relief charities and supermarkets.

This week, the charity turns 15. Ms Strickland said Hawkesbury's Helping Hands' clientele had grown from people experiencing homelessness to working families doing it tough, some of whom travel well outside their area to receive support.

The charity receives donated food from supermarkets and food relief organisations. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

"There can be two-income families who still can't afford to eat, meet their mortgage, meet their rent," Ms Strickland said.

"Interestingly enough, our fastest-rising demographic is actually The Hills, which most people always consider an affluent area."

No direct government funding

People like mother-of-three Paula Maher, who also looks after her two grandchildren, know how much of a difference the charity makes.

She came into Hawkesbury Helping Hands and left with a hamper that could sort out meals for the best part of a week.

Paula Maher says the charity goes a long way when finances are tough. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

"Rent payments, car payments, water bills, electricity, everything's just haywire at the moment," Ms Maher said.

" When you don't have the money for the food you just come here to Linda's and she provides you with everything that she can. "

Despite the high-profile visits from politicians during a crisis, Ms Strickland said the charity had never been directly funded by government and was instead funded through community donations and business sponsorships.

Linda Strickland hopes HHH can keep going for at least another 15 years. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Politicians from both sides of the aisle admire the charity's work.

"HHH shows up week after week to give people affordable access to food and basics, but in times of disaster and crisis the team is extraordinarily responsive," said Labor MP Susan Templeman, whose federal seat of Macquarie includes the Hawkesbury.

"As a local charity, they understand the unique geography and the people of the Hawkesbury region."

Ms Templeman said she provided a federal grant for the organisation in 2024 aimed at their volunteers and that federal funding of at least $20 million had been given to food relief providers who were among those that donated supplies to HHH.

" The benefits of federal funding to organisations like Foodbank, Second Bite, and OzHarvest flows through to communities thanks to the work of local charities like HHH. "

Liberal NSW Member for Hawkesbury Robyn Preston said the charity made a real impact for people who did not know where their next meal might come from.

"When basic necessities are not even an option, Linda and her team of amazing volunteers fill the gap, giving practical support, reinstating dignity, showing respect and continued compassion," Ms Preston said.

"That's the difference that has earned Hawkesbury's Helping Hands the high regard that the community has for the services they provide."

Supermarkets and food relief charities supply food to the HHH building. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Looking ahead to the next 15 years

Floods don't always move slowly, prepare now Floods can devastate large areas and it's important to know the risk of flooding at your home. Make sure your property is prepared because floods can happen quickly.

Ms Strickland said the charity was preparing for a major El Niño event that may bring hot days to the Hawkesbury by opening up her warehouse space as a relaxation zone with fans and couches for people who could not escape the heat.

The charity has made room for this by acquiring a neighbouring warehouse room where dozens of pre-wrapped crates filled with air mattresses and sleeping bags await the next disaster.

Ms Strickland said the charity was also gearing up for the next flood and had recently been given flood-proof bags that could contain half the goods of a house and stay submerged for four weeks.

“I can see myself being here for another 15 years," Ms Strickland said.

"Whether I'm here or not, because it's not about me, we have amazing volunteers.

"I think Hawkesbury's Helping Hands is a much-needed place."

title: Indigenous dads challenging stereotypes this Father's Day
text:
Across Australia this Father's Day, children will hand over homemade cards, families will crowd around breakfast tables and dads will be celebrated for the role they play in their children's lives.

But for many Indigenous fathers, that celebration sits alongside a more complicated reality.

Almost two decades after the Northern Territory intervention, Indigenous men and researchers say its shadow still lingers, reinforcing stereotypes of Aboriginal fathers as absent, irresponsible or dangerous.

Author and Kalkalgal man Thomas Mayo says those perceptions are not confined to the past.

SMS4DeadlyDads supports Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander fathers through pregnancy and early parenthood. (Supplied: SMS4dads)

"The stereotypes have been around for a long time," he said.

"We've seen them through the media, through racist cartoons that have basically told Australians that Indigenous fathers don't care about their children."

Mr Mayo said the 2007 Northern Territory intervention intensified those stereotypes.

Cartoon prompts complaints Cartoonist Bill Leak says it is "absurd" he has been accused of being racist over a cartoon portraying an Aboriginal father and son.

"The Northern Territory intervention back in the day really turned that stereotyping into a national scapegoating of Indigenous men," he said.

Mr Mayo was raising three young children at the time and remembered feeling scrutinised simply for being with them in public.

"We remember that just holding our children in a shopping centre, [we] had suspicious eyes on us as if our children needed protecting from us because we were Indigenous men," he said.

He later became a single father, gaining full custody of his children when they were four, six and seven.

"I'd iron their clothes every day and make sure that they were looked after and everything," he said.

'It's like we've gone backwards'

Mr Mayo said he believed racism towards Indigenous people had worsened since the 2023 Voice referendum.

"Since the referendum, racism has become much worse," he said.

"It's like we've gone backwards 50 years."

Richard Fletcher (right) says Indigenous fathers need support that builds on their strengths. (Supplied: SMS4dads)

Fatherhood researcher Richard Fletcher agreed the intervention had left lasting damage.

"It painted a picture that Aboriginal children were in danger from the men in the family," Dr Fletcher said.

He has spent about four decades working with fathers and helped develop the SMS4dads and SMS4DeadlyDads programs.

Dr Fletcher said negative stereotypes could add to the ordinary pressures of raising children.

"The negative perceptions become part of the sort of burden or the things that Aboriginal fathers have got to get over."

Supporting dads, not judging them

The SMS4DeadlyDads program aims to strengthen Indigenous fathers' confidence and connection with their children. (Supplied: SMS4dads)

SMS4DeadlyDads is a free text-messaging service for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander fathers across Australia.

More than 1,000 Indigenous fathers have signed up to receive information about pregnancy, children's development, supporting partners and their own wellbeing.

Gomeroi man Craig Hammond, an Indigenous lead with the program, said fathers could sometimes be overlooked during pregnancy and early parenthood.

Craig Hammond says Indigenous fathers play an important role in keeping children connected to family, culture and country. (Supplied: SMS4dads)

"Everybody's there with the mum, you know, rubbing tummy and all that, but it's about supporting the dad through this stage," he said.

Mr Hammond said he had watched fathers become increasingly involved in parenting over the years.

"It's giving dads responsibility to take action," he said.

"That's our job too."

Dr Fletcher said services should build on the strengths Indigenous fathers already had rather than approach them as a problem.

"They don't need support to tell them what they're doing wrong," he said.

" They need support to help them be the dad they want to be. "

Passing culture to the next generation

For Mr Mayo, fatherhood is about passing culture, knowledge and identity between generations.

His book Dear Son brings together letters from Indigenous men reflecting on family, masculinity and culture.

"[Dear Son] is an act of defiance that is full of love, celebrating Indigenous men and Indigenous culture," he said.

Mr Hammond said he also made sure his grandchildren knew where they came from and returned with them to country.

For Mr Mayo, this Father's Day is a chance to celebrate Indigenous dads for exactly that role.

"We should be celebrating the long history of Indigenous fatherhood passing on knowledge from generation to generation," he said.

"We continue to be good fathers right across Australia and raise good men."

Dr Fletcher agreed.

"Yes, we should shout out about it," he said.

"We should definitely celebrate."

title: The ACT's 99-year leases are expiring — what does that mean for home owners?
text:
The ACT is home to a quirky piece of legislation that means land is leased from the Commonwealth for a period of 99 years.

It means that home owners (regardless of whether they are paying off their mortgage or own their home outright) are still technically lessees, and must renew that lease at expiry.

That lease renewal comes with a fee, and owners should be notified well in advance of its due date.

But experts say no-one has ever lost their home for failing to renew, and the prospect of that happening in the future is extremely unlikely.

Why does the ACT have 99-year leases?

The origin of the leasehold system dates back to the 19th century when Australia was choosing the site of its capital city.

At the time, speculation over land was rife in other parts of the country — a practice where someone would hold or buy land, only to see its value increase, and not to build on it.

The ACT was created to resolve debate about where a national capital should be. (Supplied: Jake Badior)

"Land scandals associated with the grant of lands and speculative development were especially common in Sydney and Melbourne in the 19th century and led to heightened concern that after the long debate about the siting of the National Capital it would give rise to unseemly land speculation," a parliamentary committee tasked with reviewing the leasehold system almost 80 years after its implementation reported.

There was also a belief at that time that there would be limited funds available for the establishment of a federal government and its associated bureaucracy.

The Commonwealth thought the leasehold system would lead to "orderly" and "predictable" development of the city by placing conditions on the granting of leases.

At Canberra's naming ceremony on March 12, 1913, the foundation stones for the capital were laid and the city's name was revealed. (ABC News)

Does it apply to all land in the ACT?

Wayne Morgan, an associate professor of law at the Australian National University, said the leasehold system applied to all private and commercial property in the ACT.

"States of freehold are what exists in the rest of the country, and it's the closest thing to complete absolute ownership that we have in our system of Anglo-Australian law," Professor Morgan said.

"But because the Commonwealth government wanted to retain more control over land in the national capital, it decided instead that what it would put in place was this system of Crown leases.

"So whether that's residential, commercial, rural, it is all under this system."

The time period of a 99-year lease is not changed when a new owner purchases the property. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The year of the lease expiry can be found on the land title register of the individual property.

"Anyone who's purchased land in the ACT … they're purchasing the lease," Professor Morgan said.

"Anybody who's done that should have within the documents that they received upon purchase a copy of the Crown lease and that would also record when it was issued and when it is due to expire."

Under the legislation, the lease period does not restart no matter how many times the property changes hands.

What happens when leases expire?

Canberra is a relatively young city compared with other places in Australia. It was founded on March 12, 1913.

But the first residential and commercial leases were not auctioned off under the leasehold system until 1924.

That means many 99-year leases have only started to expire in some older suburbs in recent years.

According to Brad Maxwell from the City and Environment Directorate (CED), between 10 and 46 leases come up for expiry each year.

The leasehold system applies to all private property in the ACT. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

This year, 32 leases are due to expire.

"When these leases do come up for expiry, our team at CED write to lessees to remind them that the period's coming up soon and you do need to make an application to extend that period through an application that's called a further lease application," Mr Maxwell said.

" There will be a letter in the mailbox reminding home owners to submit that application, and that is generally sent out a few years out from expiry. So there's plenty of notice. "

He said to renew the lease for a further 99 years, an administrative fee applied of about $540 for residential properties and $4,800 for commercial properties.

Those who do not have the means to pay can access financial hardship support through the ACT Treasury, but Mr Maxwell said they gave years of notice in an effort to avoid such a predicament.

While all home owners should have received a copy of their Crown lease upon purchase of the property, Mr Maxwell said in the event that that was not the case, they were available for purchase through the Land Titles Office, by searching the ACT Land Information System (ACTLIS).

The national capital is unique in Australia due to its 99-year leases. (Supplied: Jake Badior)

Can I be evicted or lose my property if I don't renew?

While it is technically possible for someone to lose their property if they did not renew their lease, both Mr Maxwell and Professor Morgan said it was highly unlikely.

"I don't want to panic anybody," Professor Morgan said.

"Yes, theoretically, the government could refuse to renew a lease or vary the conditions on a lease. But as I said, that has never occurred throughout the entire history of the ACT and we would not expect it to occur.

"You can imagine the political fallout."

Mr Maxwell agreed it was extremely unlikely to occur.

"There is a consideration when considering whether to grant a further lease if the land is required for public or policy use," he said.

" [It's] very, very unlikely that is exercised, very rare that it will occur, particularly in a residential setting. "

Associate Professor Wayne Morgan says the lease renewal process should be smooth. (Supplied: ANU)

In the "unlikely situation" a landholder did not renew their lease by the end of the 99-year period, Mr Maxwell said it could be continued on a "holding-over basis".

"There's no penalty for that, but it's something that we would work closely with the lessee to finalise their further lease application as soon as possible," Mr Maxwell said.

" So there is that contingency, but we'll be working with all lessees to make sure that doesn't occur. "

Professor Morgan agreed, saying it should be a smooth process.

"But of course, if anybody has any concerns, it's always a good idea to seek legal advice," he said.

ACT residents should be notified of the up-coming lease renewal requirement well in advance. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Why do we still have this system?

Canberra is the only location in Australia that does not permit a freehold system of occupying land.

Since it was founded, the ACT has changed significantly, including moving to a system of self-government.

So with those changes, why are the 99-year leases still in place, and do the reasons for their creation still apply?

Mr Maxwell said the system did hold some value, despite being first drafted more than 100 years ago.

"It was set up to provide that opportunity for orderly planning and imposing particular terms for the use of land, so it did have value and still has value in that regard," he said.

The ACT first gained self-government in the late 1980s, but the leasehold system was retained. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

In the year before self-government began in 1989, the parliamentary committee tasked with examining it recommended the leasehold system continue.

In coming to this decision, the committee said it saw public ownership as giving government stronger tools to plan and manage Canberra in the public interest.

"Canberra land is a national heritage to be safeguarded and used for the benefit of the nation and its capital," it said.

" Leasehold tenure ensures that ownership of the land remains in the public domain for the benefit of all Australians. "

These conclusions reaffirm one consistent tension that often reappears when town planning is debated in the ACT — it is not just a home for Canberrans; it belongs to all Australians.

title: The 100 Project preserves history of Australia's centenarians
text:
When Bek Hyland sat down to interview her grandmother, Merle Moore, she found herself taken back to a time when the horse and cart were the main form of transport.

The late centenarian remembered the grief of losing a sister, and the simple joy of turning on a light switch.

"I've had a sad life, but I've got to overcome a lot of that and think of the good things, not the bad things," she said.

"Nobody had power, electricity, just kerosene lights on the centre of the table; white candles in a candlestick to get to bed with, until electricity came and then everyone was laughing."

"Unless you've been through it, you just don't know the value of lights."

There are more than 50 profiles of centenarians on The 100 Project website, including Merle Moore. (Supplied: The 100 Project website)

One of the "good things" Ms Moore got to savour before her death at the age of 106 was watching herself tell her life's story on the 100 Project, an online directory of centenarians' tales.

"We watched it a few times together over the years because she'd forgotten she'd done it," Ms Hyland said.

"She was always in awe: 'Wow, that was me, yes, that's my life, that's so great.'

"It always brought a smile to her face to know she was captured and will be remembered this way."

On Merle Moore's 100th birthday, the family held a party to celebrate her, grandson Jamie included. (Supplied: Bek Hyland)

When Ms Hyland was planning her grandma's 100th birthday party at Depot Beach on the south coast of NSW, the 100 Project caught her eye, and a couple of years later she reached out.

"Having the opportunity to simply sit with her and ask her the questions and capture her memories, it's been one of the most meaningful experiences of my life," she said.

"We did it four years ago now, and there are many more centenarians who have added their stories to it since.

"I can only imagine it's going to keep growing now that people are living longer."

The 100 Project

Filmmakers Ros Walker and John Winter are the creators of The 100 Project, which encourages people to document elders' stories for posterity.

John Winter says the subjects are often keen to tell their stories. (Supplied: John Winter)

"Often with the very old, they tend to get little grabs on Anzac Day or on special occasions when you see them blowing out candles and things like that," Mr Winter said.

"But I've discovered centenarians have great stories to tell and they're very keen on telling them."

Potential participants are asked to fill in an online form.

Nominating a centenarian is an easy step-by-step online process. (Supplied: 100 Project website)

If the nomination is accepted, they can upload their own videos, which are edited for free, or the project team may choose to do the interview themselves.

"We probably interviewed half of the centenarians we've got, but families can use the online tutorials, their smartphones and our questions to interview the centenarian," Mr Winter said.

" We're interested in talking to people that have lived for 100 years and asking their opinion on how things are going in the world, and in the future as well. "

With no plans other than sharing online through social media, The 100 Project stores the content for posterity, for current and future Australians.

Video versus audio

The 100 Project is not the only digital collection of Australia's spoken history.

The Memory Tapes podcast by the National Library of Australia presents a collection of audio interviews with Australians that dates to 1957.

Shirleene Robinson has been hosting The Memory Tapes throughout August at the National Library of Australia in Canberra. (Supplied: National Library of Australia)

Curator Shirleene Robinson said the stories contained in the 58,000 hours of recorded history included famous people and ordinary Australians as well.

"There are people in that collection who can take us back to stories of seeing the convicts with lashes on their backs and so on, so it really is an extraordinary resource for all Australians," Dr Robinson said.

Dr Robinson said there was a growing interest in genealogy, ancestry and living history.

"It's important we understand the history of our own country, and it's also important we understand the histories of our family, of who we are as well," she said.

The aural historian said it could be easier to capture people's stories without filming them.

"I think it's a lot easier to have somebody relax and share their story if it's only audio than if they're also being filmed at the same time," she said.

"People really are searching for something that is real, that is genuine and authentic where you know you're listening to something that was recorded face-to-face, perhaps in 1987 or just this year, that's really powerful."

Don't interrupt!

Loading...

For anyone looking to record the story of an elderly or medically unwell loved one, Mr Winter had some simple advice.

He said the key was finding a quiet location and not interrupting the subject.

"Allow them space after they've answered a question because often, after the silence, comes the best answer."

title: Phase two of the Kiss-era Wallabies is about to begin. There is one lingering concern
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Phase two of the Kiss-era Wallabies is about to begin. There is one lingering concern Iain Payten September 6, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Peering into a laptop during a virtual press conference after a win over Argentina on Sunday morning, Wallabies coach Les Kiss was explaining why he’d been so persistently funky with selections - and substitutions - during his first five weeks in charge. In a run of four Tests against Japan and Argentina, Kiss made an average of eight changes to his starting team for each game. And then when games were underway, the coach responded to injuries and substitutions by sometimes rearranging several positions at a time. Loading “There’s a combination we’ve never seen before - or will see again,” Stan commentator Sean Maloney said when looking at a backline of Kalani Thomas, Ryan Lonergan, Len Ikitau, Isaac Henry and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii. Injuries informed some of that jigsaw - and we learned Lonergan is a tidy No.10 - but Kiss said there was a method to the madness.

Advertisement

“Some of the things we’re trying to work on is to make ourselves a bit future-proof,” Kiss said. “So we become adaptable in those spaces.” There was a risk to Kiss’ strategy. Changing half of the team each week could have exposed the team to a lack of cohesion against sides with proven capacity to beat big nations. Les Kiss poses with the Wallabies in a team photo ahead of the Mendoza Test. Getty Images And things definitely spluttered at times, but not enough to bring on disaster. Three wins and a draw from four Tests is no small feat, and there is credit due, particularly to the forwards, who have swiftly become the centre of the Wallabies’ game. There also needs to appreciate the difficulty of doing it all mostly on the road - particularly in Argentina.

Advertisement

As he did ahead of the Mendoza Test, Kiss also indicated to the laptop that the time had come for the experimentation phase to end, and the start of a more settled team phase to start. There is just over one year until the 2027 Rugby World Cup, and history tells us World Cup winners are usually playing together in a discernible combination in the year prior. Loading “I was just talking to the coaches earlier. We feel that some of the decisions we’ve made over these four or five weeks, we got a lot of good information from it,” Kiss said. “That’ll certainly narrow the mindset in terms of how we go forward for sure. It was important that this whole group knew we were going to back them. They knew that we were going to challenge them in many different ways ... we’ll get a lot of pay from that down the road.”

Advertisement

Next up is a clash with the Springboks in Perth on September 27. The Boks will be coming out of the four-Test series against the All Blacks battered, but also battle-hardened. Kiss has some tough calls to make about who makes his discernible combination. There are surplus options in the back row, front row and centres. That depth is a bonus. More worryingly, the back three has become a mess, with only Max Jorgensen a certain pick. Len Ikitau of Australia takes on Faustino Sanchez Valarolo of Argentina. Getty Images Perhaps the most concerning part for Kiss and the Wallabies, in both the form seen in the four Tests and the selection picture for the future, is the wobbly game management from the halves and fullback. The Wallabies have at times looked unstoppable with the ball, when rolling downhill in the rival half. The power and pace of forward runners, via Lonergan’s sharp service, is on par with any side in the world.

Advertisement

But the Wallabies have also struggled to play with composure when on the back foot, and be smart and efficient when exiting their own half. Time and again, errors in getting to a good kick and playing down the other end have resulted in the Wallabies putting themselves under pressure. Worryingly, those errors even came in batches. Pablo Matera’s second, go-ahead try in Mendoza came after four botched exits in a row. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii in action against Argentina. Getty Images No matter how good your defence or your ability to win turnovers, the modern game is now like the NFL: if you spend too much time in your half, you’ll concede points. Tom Wright’s chronic impulsiveness from fullback is also manna from heaven for rivals hoping for unearned access to the red zone.

Advertisement

“The problem is at times we’re probably not just managing the game away from our third of the pitch enough times,” Kiss said. “We’re just probably three steps forward in controlling the game and then suddenly one or two steps (back), we’re back on our back foot again.” Related Article Opinion

Wallabies Les Kiss knows his strongest Wallabies side. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author The problem Kiss faces is that the simple solution - picking the best game manager - could be off the table for the Boks’ clash. Carter Gordon has shown himself to be the most reliable option for steering the Wallabies around. But at the ground where one of his mentors, Quade Cooper, suffered a ruptured Achilles tendon in 2022, Gordon hobbled off with an ankle injury and went for scans. That’s usually a precursor to bad news, meaning Kiss may need to turn back to Declan Meredith or Ben Donaldson to be the game manager to meet the Springboks.

Advertisement

After five weeks under Les Kiss, the Wallabies have shown they have depth, forward power, a mostly strong set piece, and the belief to defend for long periods and win turnovers. They’ve also shown they have the tendency to shoot themselves in the foot. When you’re playing South Africa and New Zealand, you can’t give them any help.

title: Farage says Britain is broken and only Reform can fix it. Now the pressure is on to deliver
text:
Nigel Farage, in the party’s trademark light blue, is under pressure in parliament and the media. He’ll also have to address the palpable frustration among ordinary people about the state of their communities.

From a distance, it is easy to dismiss Reform as an extreme movement that wants to overturn British politics with radical change. Up close, however, the members are ordinary people with everyday concerns.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Birmingham: A feudal king is striding through the crowd as thousands of Reform UK members gather to hear their leader, Nigel Farage, remind them that they are on a mission to save Britain. The king is dressed in faux chain mail, a crown and a red cloak embroidered with lions – a reminder of the country’s glorious past. And he is an instant hit with the Reform faithful. Chris Luck has come to the annual Reform conference dressed as Richard the Lionheart, famous for defending English territory and waging crusades against Muslim enemies. Luck, 62, enjoys medieval re-enactments when he is not working in the distribution business from his home in Bracknell, west of London. His reason for wearing this outfit today, he says, is to remind Britain what makes it great. “The main problem with this country is immigration,” he tells me. “That’s the thing that needs to get sorted out. And once they get that sorted out, that’s going to affect everything else that’s wrong with the country, because all the money is being wasted on them.” Chris Luck says he dressed as Richard the Lionheart to remind Britain what makes it great. David Crowe By them, he means migrants. He wants a complete stop to unauthorised arrivals. He believes the government has set up an “invitation machine” by offering too many welfare and housing incentives for asylum seekers who come by boat across the English Channel. And he blames Labour and the Conservative Party: “They’re all traitors.” There is plenty of passion for the Reform movement here in this vast conference hall on the edge of Birmingham, where party members are spending two or three days to see the leaders they admire. Some are enjoying some political cosplay by dressing up, especially in the party’s trademark light blue, but most look like the people you see on an average English high street. Whatever they are wearing, they share Luck’s concern about migration. From a distance, it is easy to dismiss Reform as an extreme movement that wants to overturn British politics with radical change. Up close, however, the members are ordinary people with everyday concerns. And that is exactly why the party remains so significant even when Farage is tainted by scandals over donations from wealthy crypto investors and the sudden resignation of two aides caught on camera talking about taking money from foreign donors.

Advertisement

Farage is under pressure in the parliament and the media, but that’s not the only pressure that counts. A much more powerful force, over time, is the palpable frustration among ordinary people about the state of their communities. As society changes, tension grows. And people will demand to be heard. Susan Morrell, a small business owner, was a member of the Liberal Democrats, the UK’s middle-of the-road party, for 32 years. She served on the local council in her town of Coalville, in the English Midlands, and supported Labour at times, but she has joined Reform because she worries about the degradation of government services. She believes migration is a key problem. “It’s overwhelming the country and we’ve got to be realistic about it,” she says. Susan Morrell, who believes migration is a key problem, in front of a poster of Farage urging members to consider standing for election for the party. David Crowe Morrell is the daughter of a migrant who came to England from Austria in the 1950s. She is not against migration, but she is worried about the scale of the influx in recent times when she sees the change in the nearby city of Leicester. “I’ve always been kind of in the centre of politics, but I’ve moved a little bit more to the centre right,” she says. “I’ve seen how Leicester has changed over the last 10 years. There are an awful lot of people that just hang around, and they’ve obviously not got anything particular to do, and they’ve not come in on work visas. They’ve not gone the proper route.” When Morrell’s father required medical help last month, she struggled to get what he needed. He was sent home without a care package, she says, even though he had broken his sternum and ribs. When she broke her foot in June, she says, she was sent home from the medical walk-in centre and had to drive herself in pain.

Advertisement

“I’m thinking, well, this is just not right. You don’t know it until you experience it, what’s happening on the front line. And it’s not that the staff are awful people, it’s just that they’re overwhelmed. “I think that’s what’s really, really done it. It’s the sheer numbers for me.” In Britain, as in Australia, hospitals and aged-care homes depend heavily on workers from overseas. Of the 1.5 million workers in the National Health Service, around 325,000 were born overseas, according to the House of Commons Library. That represents about one in five health workers. (The biggest source countries are India, the Philippines, Nigeria, Ireland and Poland). Loading The challenge for Britain, and the source of frustration for Reform members, is that life does not seem to be improving as a result of migration. Whether the complaints are about healthcare, or drug addicts on the high street, or rubbish in the alleyways or slow progress on building new roads, there is an overwhelming sense of decline in living standards. One of the most effective refrains from Farage captures this sense of gloom. “Nothing works any more in this country,” he says. Another refrain tells voters he is their only hope. “Britain is broken: only Reform can fix it.” Vicky Shaw, a nurse, is loud and proud at the Reform conference in Birmingham. She arrives in a light blue jacket, with a matching cowboy hat in the party colours, and she has good reason to be confident about the party’s future. She was elected as a councillor on the Crewe Town Council in May, when Reform confirmed its rise by defeating Labour and the Conservatives in many neighbourhoods.

Advertisement

Shaw says health services are under severe stress and migration has not helped, even though it has brought in some workers. “The way it’s working at the moment, there’s too many managerial roles and not enough nurses,” she says. In her view, government money is being wasted in other areas when health needs more support, and she believes the passage of asylum seekers across the English Channel has to end. “I think we should stop the boats,” she says. “I think that any government that allows it to happen has blood on their hands for every death in the channel. They could easily stop the boats – get the army, get the navy to stop them.” Vicky Shaw says health services are under severe stress and migration has not helped. David Crowe The boat arrivals make headlines every time dozens of migrants make it on to an inflatable dinghy from the beaches of France and Belgium, but the numbers vary. There were no arrivals in the week to September 4. In the final week of August, however, 616 migrants arrived on 10 boats. The rolling tally at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford shows the annual rate has fallen to about 32,000. This is down from last year but is about three times the inflow seen in 2021. The argument in Britain mirrors the years of dispute in Australia about whether asylum seekers are motivated by “push” factors from their home countries or the “pull” factors about living in London or other cities. One thing that grates on voters is that asylum seekers are often housed during processing in hotels in residential neighbourhoods, giving them a quality of accommodation beyond the budgets of most people. Steve Trevelyan, a former soldier who lives in St Austell in Cornwall, thinks the asylum seekers are responding to a signal sent out by the British government.

Advertisement

“I can’t blame them. Our governments give them an incentive to come over – housing, money, mobile phones, they put them up in five-star hotels. But you’ve got veterans on the streets who don’t get that,” he says. What is the solution? “Don’t offer these incentives. People will go to wherever they get handouts. If there are genuine cases where there are asylum or persecution, possibly [let them in]. But we do know the majority are coming over for the economic benefits.” Labour and the Conservatives have been wary of shutting down assistance for asylum seekers, given decades of support for refugees under British law. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, would face a backlash from his Labour party room if he attempted to remove benefits, but there is a live debate in Britain about whether the current law makes it too hard for border authorities to remove migrants. One factor is that migrants contesting their removal can rely on the European Convention on Human Rights, an international treaty the UK supports. This has totemic importance for Reform, which describes the ECHR as a sign of weak national government. Farage vows to remove the UK from the treaty and make sure judges have to order more asylum seekers out of the country. On the conference floor in Birmingham, Reform members name the ECHR as a key issue. But it is not the only issue. Trevelyan names “woke” politics from progressive causes, free speech and welfare as some of his concerns. We speak after he has just signed a condolence book to express grief at the death of Ann Widdecombe, the former Conservative and Reform politician who was killed in her home in July. Widdecombe made enemies with her traditional social values, especially when she argued against activists for trans rights. A man has been charged with her murder. Farage is scrambling to control the political damage from the donation scandal hanging over him and his party. On Friday morning, hours before he addressed the party conference in Birmingham, he removed the two aides caught on camera talking about funding from overseas donors, which is banned under donations law. He says the aides were suspended for “loose pub talk” but insists he and the party have done nothing wrong.
