title: ‘Caught in a trap’: The most expensive regions for insurance on Australia’s east coast revealed
text:
Megan Vicary lives where the Nepean meets the Hawkesbury River, and across the road from the Grose River.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Across the country, Australia is falling behind in adapting to the baked-in impacts of climate change. See all stories .

Megan Vicary is among the growing ranks of Australians who do not carry full home insurance. The 52-year-old moved to her 10-hectare property in Yarramundi in the Hawkesbury region nine years ago and had an insurance policy that cost her about $6000 a year. After four floods in 2022, it went up to $35,000 a year, and she could no longer justify the expense. Now, the quotes are as high as $50,000 a year, and many insurers won’t offer flood coverage at all, based on her postcode. She still has a policy, but it doesn’t cover flood. “No one’s insuring for flood,” Vicary says. “If we have a major flood, it is going to be a crisis because none of us can afford it. All the way down the riverbank, none of us are flood-covered.” The same crisis is playing out nationally as mounting climate disasters drive up insurance risk, and consumers drop their coverage, preferring to self insure or hope for a government bailout. As the United Nations reports that the goal of curbing global warming to 1.5 degrees has failed, the task of climate adaptation grows more important. Insurance is at the heart of the challenge. Across Australia, the regions with the highest insurance premiums are those with the most flood risk, and this is particularly true on the east coast, according to analysis prepared exclusively for this masthead by actuarial firm Finity. Bushfires are a factor, too, but flood is the overwhelming driver.

Advertisement

The most expensive insurance on the east coast is in the Richmond-Tweed region in the NSW Northern Rivers, when comparing large sub-state regions defined by the Australian Bureau of Statistics as statistical area 4 (SA4). In Richmond-Tweed, near the Queensland border, premiums have risen 81 per cent since January 2021. The average quote for a new policy in the region, which includes Lismore, Tweed Heads, Murwillumbah, Byron Bay and Ballina, is now $8836 a year. The most expensive insurance in Victoria by SA4 is in the Shepparton region, where the average quote is $4871 a year, up 77 per cent. The highest in Queensland is in the west of Brisbane, where home owners now pay an average of $6173, up 74 per cent. What all three regions have in common is that they were hit by devastating floods, sometimes numerous times, over the past decade, and most especially in 2022. NSW premiums are particularly high because they include the emergency services levy of between 15 and 18 per cent, which is not funded through insurance in other states. The NSW government is considering reforms. Premiums in the Cairns SA4 region have gone down over the past five years and are now an average $3985 a year. Finity principal Stephen Lau says this is because the federal government created a cyclone reinsurance pool in northern Australia to make insurance more affordable in cyclone-prone areas. The program is monitored by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

Advertisement

In some locations, it is possible to zoom in even closer to clusters of individual suburbs. Breaking down the Blue Mountains and Outer West sub-state region into three SA3 sub-regions reveals that the Richmond-Windsor area – where Yarramundi is located – has average premiums of $12,606 a year, a rise of 91 per cent over five years. Again, the main reason is flood risk. But in Victoria, the most expensive of these smaller regions is the Yarra Ranges, east of Melbourne, which has an average premium of $5183 a year, an 81 per cent rise mainly because of fire risk. Related Article Climate crisis ‘The homes we build twice’: Repair bill for climate disasters climbing faster than inflation Analysis used by the Insurance Council of Australia suggests the most vulnerable people and communities in Australia have the highest flood risk but the lowest financial and social capacity to protect their properties and families and to recover from disaster. Council chief executive Andrew Hall is hugely concerned by this trend. “When the worst happens to them, and most of the time I’m talking flooding, they just go backwards, and [that] creates this intergenerational cycle of poverty because they’re caught in a trap that they can’t get out of,” Hall says. “They can’t sell their home [because] no one buys it back. It gets rebuilt in the location it was in, or they’ve just got no money and they’re stuck trying to put together what they’ve got left. That is the big picture.”

Advertisement

About 1.4 million properties nationally face some risk of flooding, including almost 300,000 properties that face a severe-to-extreme annual flooding risk, largely in NSW, Queensland and Victoria, the Insurance Council says. The cost of dealing with natural disasters without insurance is high. Megan Vicary’s home was built nine years ago, and comprehensive insurance with flood cover now costs about $50,000 a year. Wolter Peeters Vicary’s home was built in the past nine years and sits about five metres above what is commonly referred to as the one-in-100-year flood line – though more accurately, that means there is a 1 per cent chance of flooding in any given year. The water has never risen as high as her house, but the clean-up is still a big task. Related Article Climate crisis ‘Little by little cities will have to recede’: Coastal flooding is the sleeper climate issue “Even if you don’t get floodwater in your home, when that river comes up, you’ve got all the animals that come out of everywhere – the mice, the snakes, the bugs,” Vicary says. “Mildew starts to grow in your house – I literally for weeks had to turn my air-conditioner on to get the humidity out of my house, so I didn’t have mould growing.” Her lower paddocks front the river, so she has to evacuate animals – including alpacas, sheep and horses – and then clean up for their safe return. She has spent $65,000 of her savings on replacing fences, cleaning out low-lying sheds and disposing of the debris dumped by the river, including a washing machine and half a speedboat.

Advertisement

Australia remains a relatively well-insured nation, but the protection gap is growing. The Insurance Council’s Alix Pearce wrote in a Churchill fellowship report titled Insuring Australia Tomorrow in January that, of Australia’s $US37 billion ($51.7 billion) in losses from extreme weather over the past decade, $US12 billion, or about a third, was not insured. Between 1987 and 2015, the number of properties exposed to high flood risk increased by more than 65 per cent both because of more homes being built and also climate change increasing the physical risk. The average cost to build a new house in Australia has risen by 30 per cent since 2021, faster than the cumulative inflation rate of 24 per cent over the same time frame, the Insurance Council reported this week. When damaged properties are repaired under insurance, they are held to outdated building standards, which means they will not be resilient to worsening weather. People who can afford it are taking matters into their own hands and disaster-proofing their homes. Bec Nicoll and Sarah Thomson at their nearly completed resilient home in Kialla, near Shepparton. Justin McManus Building back better Sarah Thomson, 53, and Bec Nicoll, 56, moved into their newly rebuilt home in Kialla, near Shepparton, a week ago, more than four years after they were flooded by Seven Creeks, a tributary of the Murray.

Advertisement

They are relieved and delighted, after first living in a caravan for nine months and then in a 36-square-metre shed for more than three years. They have built back better, putting in about $500,000 of their own money on top of the insurance payout. First, they had to battle with their insurance company, Allianz, for 12 months to be allowed to demolish and rebuild. “They said that it was repairable, but the slab was still wet after nearly 12 months, and we didn’t want to be putting floorboards on top of a wet slab,” Thomson says. “Negotiating with the insurer was a long, tedious, irritating process. That’s not available to a lot of people. We’ve got the ability to actually negotiate and to be able to fight for a good outcome.” Nicoll says Emergency Recovery Victoria provided teams of engineers and hygienists who recommended demolition, but Allianz “completely disregarded” the report as too generic. Eventually, the couple engaged a private engineer and researched insurance law to force the issue. Allianz chief claims officer Luke Whenman apologised if Thomson and Nicoll had had a bad experience. He said the company always looked for the best way to build back within the funding envelope, and that it could provide an extra $20,000 to boost resilience. Cash settlement was not a good option for most customers because they would be unable to find tradespeople after a disaster, he said. Sarah Thomson and Bec Nicoll spent nine months living in a caravan and more than three years in their shed. Just in McManus Thomson and Nicoll’s new house is raised on stumps and is also on a hillside, making it 1.25 metres higher than their old home and above the one-in-100-year flood level, with a buffer for climate change. They have also adhered to Passivhaus principles for temperature control and relevant bushfire codes. None of this has made a difference to their new insurance premiums. Before the flood, they were paying between $2000 and $2500. They have now found insurance for $6100 a year, having fielded some quotes as high as $18,000 a year. When shopping around, the couple found there was nowhere to disclose any of the resilience features of their new home. “When I said to a sales agent that we’ve actually rebuilt well above the mandated height for flooding in our area, he said, ‘that’s nice, I’m happy for you, but that doesn’t alter the policy’,” Nicoll says. It was a similar story for home owners in northern NSW who flood-proofed their dwellings after being inundated in 2022. Virginia Jones and her husband, Tim Lawson, in Bogangar, near Cabarita Beach, put their home on stilts, raising it so high that a full-size netball hoop stand could fit underneath. Their next-door neighbour Bernie Zietlow rebuilt his home with materials that mean it could be hosed out after a flood. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster Jones says her insurance premiums have more than doubled to about $6000 a year, despite the lower flood risk because of raising the property. Zietlow’s insurance premiums have gone up from $1000 to $4000 a year for a small home. He has priced insurance with and without the improvements, and it made no difference. This is a problem that the Housing Resilience Action Plan aims to solve. A collaboration between Finity, the Resilient Building Council, Monash University and consumer advocacy groups, the proposal is to develop a rating system for every home in Australia that insurers use when pricing premiums. Finity principal Sharanjit Paddam says the rating for each type of natural disaster would incorporate the risk profile of the area and the resilience of the actual home. “The idea … is to have a common language, so that consumers understand what the resilience of their home is to different disasters, insurers use that information to price insurance contracts, and then banks lend people money so that they can get the house to a different resilience level,” Paddam says. “When you get your renewal notice, they’ll say, ‘OK, you are three-star-rated against flood, and that has led to this pricing for your insurance premium, but if you were four-star-rated, this is what your premium would be’. Including signals like that can empower consumers to make decisions.” Lowering community risk Related Article Analysis

Climate policy The world made a ‘covenant with the future’ – and we broke it Scott Hawkins, managing director for Australasia at global reinsurance company Munich RE, says lowering the risk of events that occur every three to five years won’t significantly reduce premiums. It’s mitigating the risk of more extreme events that occur every few decades that would make the difference, he says. “Some things people can do at the home level, but some things need to be done at the community level,” Hawkins says. The Insurance Council has called for a 10-year, $30 billion flood defence fund to bolster infrastructure in 24 priority catchments nationally. The catchments were chosen because of flood risk and insurance affordability pressure. They are all in the eastern states. Hall says the government has the right idea with the Hazards Insurance Partnership, which is designed to fund community and household infrastructure that can reduce risk and put downward pressure on premiums. That is world-leading, Hall says, because the government persuaded insurance companies to provide information into the program, whereas in other developed jurisdictions such as the United States, governments had to sue to get access to the commercially sensitive data. Related Article Electricity Bruce’s home was ‘like a tent’. A new energy rating is guiding upgrades The government also created the Disaster Ready Fund, which was $200 million a year, though it has recently been reduced to $142.4 million. “Again, huge tick, very smart idea,” Hall says. “The problem with it is that … so far… they’re programs like teaching people about bushfire awareness or building cyclone shelters.” Hall says there would be more downward pressure on premiums if the money were spent on hard infrastructure and community-level defences, such as flood levees. title: Billionaire’s $6.3m ‘bride price’ stunt could backfire
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsBillionaires Opinion Billionaire’s $6.3m ‘bride price’ stunt could backfire

Shuli Ren September 6, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just when Bitcoin seemed to be breaking out of its long winter, a publicity stunt by one of the crypto industry’s most prominent billionaires is raising questions as to whether this asset class should be in mainstream investors’ portfolios. Justin Sun, the Trump family’s earliest and biggest crypto backer, is suing a Chinese actress and her parents to recover what he describes as a bride price of 30 million yuan ($6.3 million). In a long essay posted on X, titled “My Girlfriend Jing Tian,” he recounts their relationship and portrays Jing as high-maintenance and money-hungry. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun has come under heavy fire for his latest stunt. Bloomberg This dispute has captivated Chinese society and the crypto world. The original August 27 X post alone has garnered 40 million views. In response, Jing wrote on Chinese social media Weibo, where she has more than 26 million followers, that she would never trade love for money and believes that justice would prevail. With an estimated net worth of $US8.3 billion, Sun is an expert in creating media buzz, sometimes as a way to boost the value of his business dealings. He is known for spending $US6.2 million at Sotheby’s on a conceptual artwork composed of a fresh banana stuck to a wall — and eating it in front of reporters afterwards.

Advertisement

The crypto billionaire is also litigious, suing World Liberty Financial, a crypto project co-founded by President Donald Trump, for extortion after their business associations turned sour. The company counter-sued for defamation. He also previously sued Bloomberg for reporting on his wealth, but ultimately voluntarily dismissed his case. But is this publicity stunt smart? Flamboyance doesn’t bode well when the Chinese government embraces common prosperity and is keen to rein in capital flight. In the well-crafted essay — the 36-year-old won a national writing competition in 2007 that secured him a spot at the prestigious Peking University — Sun spent pages flaunting his wealth. He’s especially fond of his Airbus A330, estimated to be worth $US200 million, boasting that the Maldives airport is too small for the private plane and the islanders at Tenerife off West Africa had never seen anything like it. Chinese actress Tian Jing has appeared in films such as 2017’s Kong: Skull Island. AP The public backlash in China was almost immediate, with prominent influencers calling Sun vengeful and a social outcast (crypto trading is illegal in China). Over the weekend, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who was instrumental in Sun’s early success, suggested he tone down the rhetoric.

Advertisement

After all, we don’t need to look far to see how Beijing feels about flashy displays of wealth. In 2022, regulators asked the entire brokerage industry to implement pay cuts after the wife of a junior trader at China International Capital Corp. drew public ire by revealing her husband’s monthly salary on social media. Finance executives’ compensation only started to bottom out last year. China more recently has been cracking down on capital flight, banning unauthorised offshore issuance of yuan-pegged stablecoins. These cryptocurrencies allow people to move money internationally without sharing identifying information, even bypassing stringent economic sanctions. View post on X It’s not hard to see how Sun may irritate Beijing. The bulk of his wealth stems from Tron, a blockchain system that has morphed into a global payments network that moves much more than PayPal. Nearly 40 per cent of Tether’s USDT, the world’s most-used dollar-pegged stablecoin, is transacted on Tron, which counted Asian crime syndicates among its early adopters, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Meanwhile, crypto exchange HTX, where Sun is a self-described advisor, hosts plenty of suspicious activities. It has been accused by the UK and the European Union of helping Russia move money. HTX has pushed back, saying Huobi Global SA — the first defendant in a legal claim the UK has made — is distinct from the online exchange, which is committed to full compliance worldwide.

Advertisement

At last week’s Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, Binance’s Zhao tried to strike a bullish tone, predicting that Bitcoin will soon overtake gold. But there are plenty of sceptics. Both assets are floated as potential beneficiaries of the so-called debasement trade — whereby investors seek refuge from the dollar for fear that it’s being devalued — but legally they’re miles apart. Central banks are buying gold to diversify their reserves, while the crypto industry still operates in a tight regulatory environment and as such, it can ill afford negative coverage now. title: How backyard mozzie traps curbed the spread of a flesh-eating disease in Melbourne suburbia
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive NationalVictoriaHealthcare How backyard mozzie traps curbed the spread of a flesh-eating disease in Melbourne suburbia Melissa Cunningham September 6, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first, it looked like an innocuous insect bite on the top of Sarah Fowler’s foot. The 52-year-old Brunswick woman noticed the small raised bump while staying with her parents on the Mornington Peninsula on New Year’s Day last year. Sarah Fowler was diagnosed with a Buruli ulcer last year after being bitten by an infected mosquito months earlier in Brunswick West. Joe Armao She went to a GP who prescribed her antibiotics. But the bump kept growing until it looked like a golf ball and her foot began to swell and ache. Weeks later, a doctor at hospital emergency department diagnosed her with a flesh-eating Buruli ulcer.

Advertisement

Related Article Graphic content

Good Weekend Stigma, isolation: the flesh-eating ulcer infecting hundreds more Victorians each year Last year, Victoria reported a record-breaking 426 cases of the tissue-destroying ulcer, and more than 100 infections have already been reported this year. As the state heads into the riskiest months for transmission, the landmark findings of a study from a group of researchers at The Doherty Institute and University of Melbourne could change how Australia halts the spread of the flesh-eating bacteria. As part of a world-first trial, researchers set up almost 600 specialised eco-friendly mosquito control traps, known as auto-dissemination stations, across transmission hotspots in the Merri-bek and Moonee Valley council areas targeting suburbs in the north-west including Brunswick West, Essendon and Moonee Ponds. Scientists have long believed mosquitoes are fuelling the spread of the mysterious disease by biting infected possums and then humans.

Advertisement

The skin infection is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium ulcerans. If it gets under the skin, it can grow and produce a toxin that can melt skin cells and fat. One of the lead researchers, University of Melbourne medical entomologist Dr Véronique Paris, said control stations were set up in residents’ backyards and in suburban streets to target mosquitoes breeding in small, hidden sources of water around people’s homes. Dr Véronique Paris and fellow researcher Dr Andrew Buultjens helped lead a world-first trial to halt the spread of the flesh-eating Buruli ulcer. Simon Schluter The black plastic container traps used scent and water to lure in female mosquitoes before coating them in a slow-acting larvicide powder. The insects then unwittingly carried the toxin to surrounding water sources, which could be anywhere from a neighbour’s water tank to roof gutters, killing off mosquito larvae across the entire neighbourhood. Paris said after eight weeks, between January and March 2024, mosquito egg counts plummeted by about 70 per cent in areas with the traps, effectively suppressing the entire insect population.

Advertisement

“But what surprised us most was the actual impact on the human cases of Buruli ulcer,” Paris said. Related Article Healthcare The unusual vaccination plan to halt ‘out of control’ flesh-eating disease After the trial, researchers compared Buruli ulcer cases reported in the six protected zones, which were fitted with the traps, against six nearby untouched “control areas” to measure how well the mosquito stations prevented human infections. Paris said it was a complex task given it can take many months for Buruli ulcers to develop in the skin after a person is bitten. Their analysis showed that residents in areas with traps were 83 per cent less likely to contract Buruli ulcers than those in unprotected zones.

Advertisement

Professor Tim Stinear, director of the World Health Organisation Collaborating Centre for Mycobacterium ulcerans at the Doherty Institute, said the findings, published in the Nature Microbiology scientific journal, showed for the first time that reducing mosquito populations could significantly reduce the risk of infection in people. Related Article Illness Flesh-eating ulcer ‘endemic’ in coastal town with ‘significant risk’ of spread to Sydney The microbiologist at the University of Melbourne said the study showed the traps were not only effective at controlling mosquitoes where the control stations were located, but also in surrounding areas. “We don’t have to kill all mosquitoes, that’s not the message,” Stinear said. “But this trial shows if we can reduce mozzie numbers by simple control measures, then we can measurably reduce transmission risk of the disease.” Stinear said even adopting simple mosquito control measures at a community level, such as using insect repellent, covering water tanks, installing fly screens and eliminating breeding sites around the home, could reduce the risk of infection.

Advertisement

Sarah Fowler was shocked to discover she had been bitten by a mosquito months before the strange bite even appeared, while she was living in the hotspot of Brunswick West. The antibiotics treated the ulcer – but things got worse before they got better. “Once you start the antibiotic treatment, it pulls the infection out,” the freelance consultant said. “There was a hole about the size of a 50¢ piece on my foot full of yellow pus. It was otherworldly looking at my foot and thinking that was on my body.” Several of her neighbours also had identical ulcers.

Advertisement

Fowler, who now has a large scar on her foot, welcomed the findings of the study. “It’s great these traps work because it is one of those things where prevention is so important,” she said. “You can’t nip it in the bud once you’ve got it. You have to go through the gruelling cycle of the infection coming out of the wound.” Director of the Western Public Health Unit in Victoria Dr Finn Romanes said there had been a 350 per cent increase in Buruli ulcer infections in the past five years across the north-west and western suburbs, where the number of cases soared from 35 in 2021 to 123 last year. “This is very significant and serious infection,” he said. “We still don’t know how it first got in, but it is really clear that it’s spreading from possums through mozzies to humans.” Romanes said high-risk suburbs grew from 12 last year to 14 this year, with Parkville and Williamstown emerging as new hotspots.

Advertisement

Related Article Science The buzz on Mosquito myths: what works to repel them and what doesn't He said the severe ulcer initially manifests as a persistent sore that will not heal, but if it is not treated with antibiotics, the bacteria slowly grows and the wound gets bigger. He urged people, particularly those living in high-risk areas, to ask their doctor for a swab test if they notice a non-healing sore. “People can suffer quite significant skin loss or deformity and sometimes even need a skin graft,” he said. He described the trial’s findings as a “moment of opportunity for public health action”.

Advertisement

“This study describes the real first urban-setting intervention that we know of which prevents transmission across a neighbourhood area,” he said. The insect traps used in the study are not yet available for purchase in Australia, but regulatory approval for their use is imminent. Romanes said authorities should explore all options, including using them for pilot schemes or free distribution of the traps to residents in high-risk zones. There were only 32 cases of the disease in 2010. In 2021, the flesh-eating ulcer spread from the Mornington and Bellarine peninsulas to inner Melbourne and, then in September 2023, a case was identified in Batemans Bay, signalling the leap of the disease to southern NSW. In 2023, infectious disease experts revealed possums would be vaccinated against the Buruli ulcer to control what they described as an astounding surge of flesh-eating disease across Victoria.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Insects The fluorescent red mozzies that could protect us from other blood-hungry biters After many years of studying Buruli ulcers, Stinear still found it remarkable that the tropical skin disease was spreading through the suburbs of Melbourne. “Thirty years ago, we didn’t really know how to detect it, treat it, or how it was spread,” he said. “Now a group of Australian researchers have answered all of those issues, and we’re moving to a bold place of well, let’s see if we can largely eliminate Buruli ulcer in Victoria.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point
text:
Advertisement

BusinessConsumer affairsEnergy ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point Nick Toscano September 6, 2026 — 12:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia has passed its tipping point in the shift away from petrol and diesel cars, Chinese auto giant BYD says, as new national sales figures show battery-electric models outsold petrol-powered vehicles last month for the first time. Australians bought 27,078 fully electric vehicles, accounting for one in four new car sales – edging out petrol vehicles (25,824) and diesel models (23,608), industry figures showed last week. When plug-in hybrids are included in the count, battery-powered cars accounted for 36 per cent of the market, while combined sales of petrol and diesel vehicles tumbled below the 50 per cent mark. Conventional hybrids made up the remainder. BYD electric vehicles unloaded at Port Melbourne. Ruby Alexander Auto executives and analysts describe the shift as a milestone for a nation that has trailed many other markets in embracing EVs.

Advertisement

“The pendulum has swung – the shift is now absolute,” said Paul Ellis, a spokesman for BYD. “It’s going to continue to increase.” Until recently, Australia had widely been considered a laggard in the uptake of electric vehicles, held back by limited model choice, high prices relative to other markets, and concerns among some consumers about whether battery-powered cars had the power and the range to cover vast distances. Related Article Electric vehicles Electric cars are taking off in Australia. Charging stations are the next challenge But electric vehicle sales have surged this year, as more Australians have sought to insulate themselves from sharply rising petrol and diesel prices due to the war between the United States and Iran cutting off global oil supplies. At the same time, an influx of lower-cost Chinese models has brought EV prices down, to be competitive with piston-powered vehicles. Ellis said consumer attitudes had shifted, reducing reluctance about EV uptake, as more Australians gained experience with electric cars.

Advertisement

“Myths have been busted,” Ellis said. “People are seeing first-hand that they are easier to drive, offer better performance, and word has been spreading.” The shift is a tailwind for efforts to slash vehicle emissions, which are polluting the atmosphere and worsening global warming. However, the pace of change poses a new challenge for governments, the auto industry and electricity companies : ensuring there are enough public chargers to cater for this year’s influx. Related Article Energy Can Australia dodge the next Iran oil shock? More than 80,000 electric vehicles had hit the road in Australia in the past three months alone, said Riz Akhtar, founder of consultancy firm Carloop. Akhtar said August 2026 sales were the “clearest sign that drivers were sick of paying high prices at the fuel pump ... going full electric and ditching petrol or diesel cars altogether.” Drivers were “making the switch faster than ever”, but fast-charging infrastructure was failing to keep up, he added. Carloop data shows NSW had 515 fast-charging sites as of last month, while Victoria had 396. “That’s going to be the biggest challenge as we expect over 30,000 more electric vehicles on Victoria’s roads, leading up to Christmas,” Akhtar said.

Advertisement

BYD’s Ellis said some prospective EV buyers were concerned about access to public charging points, not for their regular daily commute, but for longer regional road trips. “We’ve gone from ‘range anxiety’ to ‘charging anxiety’ – ‘Is there going to be a charger in Bendigo when I go there for the weekend? Will the chargers be available? Am I going to have to queue?’ “Infrastructure needs to be increased – it’s happening rapidly, but probably not quickly enough to match sales.” Last month, a major new survey of more than 42,000 members of the National Roads and Motorists Association (NRMA) found drivers of petrol and diesel vehicles were now more anxious about high fuel costs than electric vehicle owners were about funding a place to charge. NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury said the ascending sales figures showed that longstanding barriers to EV adoption were steadily falling, and 2026 would be remembered as a tipping point. “This is not a flash in the pan,” Khoury said. Toyota remained Australians’ most popular car brand in August, with 19,712 sales, down 5 per cent from a year earlier, according to the monthly sales figures from the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries and Electric Vehicle Council. In second place was BYD, up 68 per cent to 8231, followed by Tesla, up 160 per cent to 7685.

Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen said August’s EV sales surpassing petrol cars for the first time was a “landmark moment”. “Australians have seen through the scare campaigns and are voting with their wallets for cars that are cheaper to run, cleaner and reduce their exposure to international petrol prices shocks,” he said. title: 'Titan of Australian sport': Boxer Tony Mundine honoured at heartfelt Redfern memorial
text:
IN BRIEF Australian boxing great, Tony Mundine, passed away on 30 August from a heart attack.

Mundine remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions.

WARNING: This article contains the name and image of an Aboriginal person who has passed away.

Respected Bundjalung boxer Anthony 'Tony' Mundine OAM has been remembered as an "unwavering anchor" of strength and determination at an emotional ceremony in Sydney's Redfern.

Crowds gathered at Redfern Oval on Saturday morning to pay their respects to Mundine, who died from a heart attack on 30 August — aged 75.

His coffin was carried to a small stage — decorated with a large bouquet and the Aboriginal flag proudly draped across the top.

On the side, the dark wood was printed with a pair of boxing gloves and a gold rabbit, a nod to Mundine's loyal, lifelong love of the South Sydney Rabbitohs.

Bundjalung and Gadigal man Craig Madden, nephew to "Uncle Tony", welcomed guests to Country.

He recalled the life of a man who, at 15, came to Sydney to chase his dreams "into the ring".

Madden described Mundine as the "backbone" of their family.

"Steady, loyal and always there when you needed him. He was strong and staunch, yet humble, kind and generous beyond measure," he said.

"He always made room for a yarn and a laugh, or a quiet word when someone needed comfort."

"He was not a man who wasted words; the ones he shared carried wisdom, warmth and strength ... he shared lessons about life that stayed with you —leaving you feeling hopeful, grounded and ready to face what was to come next."

Tony Mundine's commitment to community lasted his entire life. Supplied by the Mundine Family. Source: Supplied / The Mundine Family

Mundine's nephew, Matthew Mundine, delivered the eulogy.

He reflected on Mundine's "quiet resilience, unwavering integrity and deep strength of character" that saw him become a "titan of Australian sport".

Acknowledging the legend's achievements in the ring, Mundine Jr said his "greatest victory" was the establishment of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym and the Tony Mundine Hostel.

"He built far more than physical places — he built sanctuaries of hope," said Mundine Jr.

"For generations of community and young people, especially Aboriginal youth seeking direction, safe housing or a second chance, Tony offered a home away from home."

A "steady anchor", Mundine was a "deeply devoted" family man and a "loyal and steadfast" friend.

"Your fight may be done, but your victories are eternal — and your legacy will never fade."

Mundine's four children, Kelly, Natalie, Anthony and Kiah, also paid tribute to their father.

His youngest child, Kiah Tony Mundine Atkins, described her father as "positive, friendly, kind and happy", a man who "loved people" and deeply loved his grandchildren.

She recalled his cheekiness, his pride in his bright red car he constantly washed, and his funny sayings, "stone the crows, and everybody was a cowboy".

"Whenever I would ask my Dad, 'How are you, Dad?' He would say, 'I'm cruising like a butterfly'," she said.

"Keep cruising like a butterfly, Dad. I love you."

Mundine's eldest, Natalie Carr-Mundine, said her Dad had a special way of "touching people's lives".

"His legacy isn't measured by the titles he has won, or the fights he fought," she said.

"It's measured by the people he has inspired, and looking here today, he's inspired quite a lot of you."

Former boxer and Mundine's only son, Anthony Mundine Junior said he aspires to be like his father.

"If I can be half the man he was in his life, I'm doing alright," he said.

READ MORE Vale Tony Mundine, the champion who inspired generations

Four of Mundine's grandsons spoke, with Jade Mundine Atkins describing his Pop as their "world".

"I'm incredibly proud to be his grandson."

Family members, Lowanna Mundine and Birrpai Elder Uncle Heath Bugg also shared tributes alongside Nick Barnett, Mundine's closest friend of fifty years.

The memorial also heard from friends, colleagues and competitors from Mundine's boxing career, including ringside doctor Dr Lou Lewis, IBF World Super Featherweight Champion Barry Michael and boxing trainer and International Boxing Hall of Fame inductee Johnny Lewis.

Tribal Warrior CEO Shane Phillips shared reflections on the importance of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym for Redfern's Aboriginal community, and Aboriginal Hostels CEO Shane Hamilton and Liz Simpson, who has managed the Tony Mundine Hostel for almost two decades, spoke about its impact on young Aboriginal men.

A young Tony Mundine ahead of his 1974 fight against American Bennie Briscoe. Source: Getty / Universal / Corbis / VCG

'A proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil'

Born on 10 June 1951, Mundine was "a proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil" — a small community on Bundjalung Country near Grafton in northern NSW.

He moved to Redfern at 15-years-old, following his talent in rugby league. But it was training in Ern McQuillan's Newtown gym that turned him to boxing.

Over 15 years, Mundine won 80 out of 96 fights and secured two Commonwealth titles. He remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions: middleweight, light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight

He cemented his status as a champion in 1974, when he challenged Argentina's Carlos Monzón for the WBA world middleweight title.

Mundine shared his gift, training others including his son Anthony Mundine Jr and grandson Rahim Mundine.

In 1986, he was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia for his dedication and service to the sport of boxing and Aboriginal youth.

"Whether it was at the many national events and gatherings, or on The Block in Redfern, Coluzzi's Café in Kings Cross or in our family homes, Tony gave so much of himself to others," his family said in a statement after his passing.

"His legacy will live on through the many people he encouraged, mentored and inspired throughout his life."

title: Where's the snow? Could 2026 be Australia's worst season?
text:
IN BRIEF Snow depth has reached a record low with five ski resorts closing operations almost a month early.

The unusually warm winter is believed to be the cause of the short season.

Australian ski resorts are being forced to close a month early due to record-low snow depth.

Snowy Mountain's Spencers Creek hit a historic Australian low, recording a snow depth of 31.2 centimetres on 3 September.

The peak depth was 94.5cm on 13 August — the third lowest depth recorded in the region since 1954.

On average, peak depth is recorded in the first weeks of September. From the 1950s to the 1970s, the average depth in the first week of September was just over 180 centimetres — compared to the 120cm average from 2020 to 2025.

Deep Creek and Three Mile Dam also recorded record-low snow depths in 2026.

The 2026 ski season was the shortest on record, with five of Australia's ski resorts already shutting the slopes.

Only three of the eight mainland ski resorts in Australia remain open — Perisher, Thredbo and Mount Buller.

The unusual winter warmth can be attributed to a multitude of weather behaviours, including El Niño, above-average sea surface temperatures, limited cold air in frontal systems and the ongoing impacts of climate change.

title: Australian drone team arrives in Nepal as search for missing continues

Australia is throwing more resources at search and rescue efforts in flood-devastated Nepal, with drone operators and victim identification experts joining the operation.

Australian rescue teams have landed in Nepal to join the search for those still missing after catastrophic floods swamped the country in August.

The 15-person specialist team landed in the capital late Friday, with additional support, including victim identification specialists on the way following a request for assistance from Nepali authorities.

A glacier collapse near Nepal's border with Tibet on 26 August triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.

At least 36 Australians remain missing, with the federal government holding grave concerns for their welfare.

On the Tibetan side of the border, the death toll rose to 31 on Friday, an increase of 10 since the previous tally, according to Chinese state media.

"Their drones will give search and rescue teams critical information about areas that may be inaccessible or too dangerous to reach from the ground.

"They have an important job ahead of them. I wish them a safe deployment and, most importantly, a safe return home."

The drone technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify anyone trapped.

DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and contact next of kin where appropriate.

Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers provided the latest update on the missing Australians on Friday, confirming that two more citizens were found safe.

It brings the number of Australians found since the catastrophic floods to seven, after five were confirmed safe on Wednesday.

Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane also arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.

More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.

title: The UN has backed a new world map that makes Africa bigger and the US smaller
text:
In brief The UN has voted in favour of adopting a new world map.

The new map updates the centuries-old Mercator projection to a "more accurate" scale.

The United Nations General Assembly voted Saturday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.

Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the United States voted against it and six other states abstained.

The new map — known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection — "is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," the resolution said.

It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.

Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps "guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions."

"They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."

The United States, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility."

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems ... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.

'Distorted representation'

The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate — in part due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map.

It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America.

A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018. It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

The Mercator projection has been the default map of the world since the 1500s, but it greatly distorts the size of many continents. Source: AAP / Mary Evans

"Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe," one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency in 2025.

France — which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map — announced Saturday that it would abandon the Mercator projection.

In that map, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he said. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."

The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties.

title: Why the 'great Aussie summer' may become a thing of the past
text:
Last summer, Paris Brooke watched in horror as a bushfire blazed through the national park across the lake from her township of Mallacoota in north-east Victoria.

The town wasn't directly at risk, but she knew what the impact would be.

"The camp park emptied out overnight, leaving businesses that depend on summer tourism stuck with unused supplies and staff, but no more tourists," Brooke tells SBS News.

The exodus was reminiscent of the summer of 2019-20, when Australia's Black Summer bushfires swept through and devastated the beachside town.

Mallacoota was among the hardest-hit areas. Apocalyptic-looking scenes of residents and holidaymakers sheltering in boats off the coast, under a red sky thick with smoke, were broadcast around the world.

While Brooke hasn't necessarily seen a slowdown in holidaymakers to the town since, she believes stays are shortening and worries the increased likelihood of extreme weather will hit summer trade long-term.

It's why she set up the Wilderness Collective, a community not-for-profit aimed at helping locals build new skills and businesses to reduce reliance on summer tourism.

"People are much more aware of natural disasters such as bushfires or droughts," she says.

Catastrophic fire conditions last summer burned through tens of thousands of hectares, destroyed multiple homes and other structures and forced widespread evacuations in central Victoria alone. Source: Getty / Jesse Thompson

On the same day last summer, climate scientist Linden Ashcroft was on the beach in Mallacoota. She recalls her kids playing in the water as embers and burnt leaves fell around them.

"It was pretty heartbreaking and terrifying. Everyone was really creeped out, and the town was covered in smoke," she says.

It left her with a lasting sense of cognitive dissonance — this is not how summer is supposed to feel.

That feeling is now rippling around the country, reaching far beyond places like Mallacoota that are historically prone to bushfires.

"Black Summer 2019–2020 was a real step change; it made people face the reality that summer can't just be carefree anymore," Ashcroft says.

You could call it the end of summer as we know it — or an evolution.

Climate Council director and academic Lesley Hughes says the changing climate is reshaping Australians' notion of summer: instead of looking forward to it, people increasingly feel apprehensive.

"They dread the heatwaves, the bushfires, not being able to do the things they used to. Climate change is stealing the part of the year Australians looked forward to most."

With higher temperatures and more extreme weather events becoming a fixture of the holiday season in parts of the country, could this signal the end of 'great Aussie summer'?

How our summers are changing

Australia is now 1.5C warmer on average than it was a century ago, according to the National Climate Risk Assessment. It's driving more extreme heatwaves and dangerous fire weather.

Monash climate scientist Andrew Watkins, former head of the Bureau of Meteorology's long-range forecast team, says the expected shifts will likely be dramatic.

"Heatwaves will cover larger areas, happen more frequently and grow more intense, with longer fire seasons stretching into autumn and spring. Rainfall will be less frequent but more intense, raising flash flood risk. Tropical cyclones may become less frequent but more severe," he tells SBS News.

Source: SBS News

Rising humidity is also driving up "wet-bulb temperature" — a combined heat-and-humidity measure that determines how well sweat can cool the body. Watkins says high readings — when sweat stops evaporating because the humidity is too high — put children and the elderly at particular risk.

"The temperature might only be 35, but if the wet-bulb is up to 25, you're going to put your body under a huge amount of stress."

Looking ahead to this summer, the Bureau of Meteorology has forecast a strong El Niño — generally meaning hotter, drier conditions — which it expects will mainly affect parts of Australia's east and south-east, raising the risk of drought and bushfires.

As extreme heat becomes more commonplace in Australia, other countries face similar conditions. Los Angeles was hit by raging wildfires last January, and Europe endured one of its worst summers on record for fire and heat this year.

It's a trend that is unlikely to shift without major and rapid structural changes, shifting global energy use to renewables and divesting from fossil fuels to limit further global warming.

New data published this week by the UN Environment Programme showed the world has lost the fight to limit warming to 1.5C. Even the most optimistic projections now point to warming of at least 1.8C — locking in more extreme weather, ecosystem loss and sea-level rise.

Reorganising the year

As projections worsen, experts are turning their attention to health risks.

Hughes at the Climate Council says the impacts of excess heat on the body can creep up slowly, and are especially dangerous for the elderly, the young, and those with heart or respiratory conditions.

She suggests more public awareness of the risks associated with heat stress is needed, but she's also calling for something more radical: reframing the calendar year to keep more of us inside during the country's hottest months.

Maybe a lot of summer would be better spent indoors, in air-conditioning, working, and leisure time moved to spring and autumn.

"Maybe our biggest school holidays shouldn't be in January," she says, adding "that would be an enormous social change for Australia".

Not everyone can escape the heat during their workday either. Professions such as tradies, farmhands, park rangers, delivery riders and some hospitality and event workers, for example, have no choice but to endure it.

A Spanish study published in 2023 offers another perspective, instead proposing to shift the country's national holidays to align with its hottest weeks to boost productivity and reduce industrial electricity consumption. Researchers found moving Spain's traditional holiday period from August to late July — the point of peak heat damage — would cut heat-driven electricity demand by 3 per cent, lost work hours by 25 per cent, and ozone pollution by 4 per cent.

Source: SBS News

Whether holidaying or working over summer, the general advice is to find ways to stay cool, and limit outdoor time to early mornings or evenings.

Although now, some Australians are reconsidering how they spend the season altogether.

The rise of the 'coolcation'

Research suggests people are already adapting to climate change without realising it, as evidenced by the rise in 'coolcations' — holidays to cool-climate destinations.

For Australians, this might include escapes to parts of northern Europe instead of southern Europe; visiting the tropics in winter instead of summer; venturing south to New Zealand or Tasmania for a mid-summer break; or snowy escapes to the Arctic, Antarctica or Alpine villages.

Trip.com data shows a 74 per cent year-on-year jump in searches for cooler destinations since the start of 2026, spiking 237 per cent across the June–August northern hemisphere summer. Searches for flights to Iceland rose 85 per cent, as travellers favoured northern Europe over traditionally popular Mediterranean spots. In Asia, cooler destinations such as Inner Mongolia, Yunnan in China and Sapporo in Japan saw similar gains.

Cold-climate destinations like Lapland in northern Scandinavia are becoming more popular, with more people seeking fun in the cold. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Holidaygoers are also increasingly considering extreme weather events when making travel plans. Booking.com's 2026 Travel & Sustainability Report found 74 per cent of travellers now factor extreme weather into where and when they travel, and 31 per cent have cancelled a trip because of it.

In Australia, the Climate Council found 61 per cent of people are concerned about extreme weather disrupting summer holidays and are adapting — shifting from inland bush locations to the coast or travelling in cooler months.

Climate scientist Watkins is a coolcationer and spends his summers camping in Victoria's cooler high country.

"[It's about] beach holidays in spring, camping in autumn, taking more advantage of Easter. Getting up into cooler places over summer is a joy."

Travelling in cooler months isn't just about comfort, of course; it often also means fewer crowds and protecting destinations from over-tourism in mid-summer.

If you're holidaying in summer

However, travelling to far-flung places to access cooler weather may not be viable for some people. Distance and cost can be prohibitive, even for domestic travel.

Simply avoiding regional or bushfire-prone areas isn't necessarily a silver bullet either.

Ashcroft warns that heat risk in major cities can be just as dangerous.

"Urban areas get hotter due to the heat-island effect, so vulnerable people may not be better off in cities."

Australia's summers on the whole are becoming hotter, drier and more intense. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

No matter where you spend the summer months, the advice is familiar by now: watch the forecasts, have a fire or heat plan, know when to leave early if conditions turn catastrophic, and avoid driving through floodwaters or bushfire smoke, which can be as thick as fog. Sometimes that means a detour, or staying put overnight until the danger passes.

Ashcroft thinks the language around summer should change altogether to help people prepare and understand the risks.

"Seasons are baked into how we talk about our year, but they're changing, so the way we talk about them has to change too. The Bureau's new term 'severe weather season' is more honest," she says.

"Being real helps us plan and prepare."

Rethinking summer sport

As our summers become more brutal, outdoor events such as music festivals and sport events may also become more challenging.

Ashcroft questions whether it still makes sense to push elite athletes to compete in extreme heat, conditions that are "not healthy and not safe".

Joanne Bowen is CEO of Cricket for Climate, a player-led movement that aims to build resilience for community clubs and the game. She calls cricket "the canary in the coal mine" for how climate change is disrupting outdoor activities.

Grassroots clubs are already cancelling junior games on hot days, with many lacking the infrastructure and budgets to adequately light night matches.

A bone dry cricket field in Bray, England, which like much of the country experienced prolonged dry weather and extreme heat this past summer. Source: Getty / Dan Kitwood

At the elite level, players have also struggled to perform in the heat, adds Bowen.

"But it's not just about the players; fans in concrete stadiums are exposed as well."

Increasing rainfall during summer is a growing problem too, she adds.

"If there's rain, you simply can't play, and there are commercial consequences for partners and fans."

She expects more games to move to nighttime and says shifting the cricket season to winter or spring is possible, though it would clash with other codes.

Another staple of Australian summer is the Australian Open.

Tennis Australia declined to discuss the long-term viability of tennis as a summer sport or moving the Australian Open from its midsummer slot, but a spokesperson said in a statement the organisation "continues to introduce strategies to protect the safety of players in hot conditions".

These include shading, misting fans, science-based heat guidelines with real-time monitoring, and heat acclimatisation education for players arriving from overseas.

The organisation's response to heat also appears to be shifting. Back in 2014, tournament director Craig Tiley defended playing through 40C conditions, saying "we are, at the end of the day, an outdoor event", even as players required medical attention.

By contrast, this year organisers suspended play after defending champion Jannik Sinner cramped mid-match under 40C conditions, with play resuming under a closed roof.

Italian tennis player Jannik Sinner recovers from heat stress during the Australian Open in January 2026. Source: AAP / Dita Alangkara/AP

Planning for future summers

Beyond the challenge of adjusting our summer holiday plans to increasingly extreme weather, a deeper issue persists: how to curb climate change.

The best way to protect Australian summers, experts say, is to stop burning fossil fuels.

"We have to address the root cause of the problem, and Australia has a big responsibility to do that," says the Climate Council's Hughes.

Experts say adaptation can't wait: retrofitting homes with renewable energy, better resourcing emergency services and warning systems, investing in coastal protection, and upgrading infrastructure — from power grids to more public cooling and green spaces — all matter now more than ever.

Climate scientist Watkins wants to see more rigorous climate risk assessments underpin a genuine national adaptation plan, backed by coordination across all levels of government.

"The most important thing is coordinated efforts — talking with communities, business sectors, and the public to find out locally what adaptation is possible," he says.

I think we'll still have fun [in summer]. We'll just need to do things a little differently.

Back in Mallacoota, Brooke’s Wilderness Collective is helping locals to build off-season opportunities.

"We're working hard to broaden the economy, so visitors come throughout the year. Winter is actually the best time to visit; it's less crowded and the weather's beautiful," she says.

"We're starting to see visitors spread across the year, which is great, but we need more of it."

Even as Australians adapt to the new realities of summer, a trade-off is occurring.

For Watkins, adapting also means facing loss.

"There's a kind of grief that doesn't get talked about enough — grief for a place," he says.

"Many of us return to the same spots every summer, hoping our kids will see them the way we first did. But those places are changing. The National Climate Risk Assessment confirms it: huge numbers of plant and animal species are already shifting, with more change ahead.

"That sense of loss is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously."

title: This virus has evolved. Australia doesn't have a new vaccine
text:
IN BRIEF Pfizer's latest COVID vaccine targets the XFG subvariant, but it has not yet been registered for use in Australia.

Experts say Australia's vaccine update process could be streamlined as new COVID variants continue to emerge.

Australians can't yet access a COVID-19 vaccine tailored for new variants, highlighting how Australia's system tends to lag behind, as a major manufacturer confirms it has no plans to push into Australia's market.

Pfizer and BioNTech's latest COVID-19 vaccine, adapted to target the XFG subvariant, has been approved in the United States for the 2026-27 season, following international guidance to more closely match vaccines with contemporary circulating variants.

Australia does not yet have that formulation registered.

But experts say the lag is not necessarily cause for alarm, with Australia continuing to monitor circulating variants and having access to relatively recent updated vaccines.

Pfizer and BioNTech's LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was registered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods in late 2025 and became available in Australia in December.

Moderna's LP.8.1 formulation has also been registered in Australia.

Australia has updated vaccines — just not the latest formulation

The issue is therefore less about Australia going without updated COVID-19 vaccines, and more about how quickly newer formulations can be made available as the virus continues to evolve.

Professor Paul Griffin, an infectious diseases physician and clinical microbiologist, said Australia tended to lag behind some countries in updating COVID-19 vaccines.

"I think it's just some of the way we're managing those updates just means it's not quite happening as streamlined a way as we might like," he said.

"We know that some countries are able to do that a bit more quickly."

Griffin said countries with more established frameworks could update vaccines closer to real time.

"We tend to lag behind a little bit," he said.

While he said faster access would be preferable, he also stressed the importance of continuing to update vaccines as the virus changes.

Several reasons for the delay

But Sarah McGuinness, a senior research fellow at Monash University, told SBS News there was no single explanation for why a new formulation might become available overseas before it does in Australia.

She said one factor is the decisions vaccine manufacturers make about which countries to seek regulatory approval in, and when, with vaccine sponsors responsible for deciding whether to seek regulatory approval in different countries.

McGuinness also said Australia is a relatively small market compared with areas such as the US and Europe, meaning new formulations are not always brought here first.

Peter Markey, a GP and public health physician who chairs the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners' public health special interest group, said Australian authorities were continuing to monitor the virus internationally.

He said governments, researchers and the World Health Organization would be watching circulating strains and sub-strains and "looking out for vaccines to match them".

There is also an established international process for determining which variants vaccines should target.

Pfizer and BioNTech say their latest XFG-adapted vaccine follows guidance to more closely match contemporary circulating variants.

Along with Pfizer-BioNTech's XFG-adapted vaccine, updated vaccines from Moderna and Novavax-Sanofi have been approved in the US for the 2026-27 season.

AstraZeneca has confirmed to SBS News that it has no plans to release a COVID-19 vaccine for the 2026-27 season.

It withdrew its vaccine from the global market in 2024, and it hadn't been available in Australia since 2023.

What does the lag mean for Australians?

For Australians, the emergence of newer formulations overseas does not mean the vaccines currently available are ineffective.

The challenge is keeping vaccine formulations aligned with a virus that continues to evolve.

Pfizer confirmed to SBS News that its LP.8.1-adapted vaccine is registered in Australia and available to people aged six months and older.

The company has not provided a timeframe for when its newer XFG-adapted vaccine could be submitted for Australian registration.

Griffin said Australia could nevertheless look for ways to streamline the updating process.

"I think that's just where we need to consider a really streamlined way of getting those updated vaccines here and available in Australia as quickly as possible," he said.

For now, experts say Australia's vaccine system is continuing to monitor the changing virus, while manufacturers decide which updated formulations to bring to the Australian market.

title: 'Beneath their office': Why the US-Canada dispute has turned so nasty
text:
IN BRIEF Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last month after Canada rejected what it called unacceptable US demands.

Donald Trump has escalated the dispute with tariffs, personal attacks and repeated suggestions Canada should become a US state.

What began as a trade fight between two of the world's most closely connected economies has escalated into a broader confrontation over Canada's sovereignty, culture and military, with United States President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney now trading increasingly personal attacks.

The latest escalation follows the collapse of trade talks between the two countries on 21 August.

Canada walked away from negotiations after saying the US had made unacceptable last-minute demands, while the US has argued there was a deal on the table that Canada chose not to accept.

The US has since imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods, with Canada preparing retaliatory measures of its own.

Since then, the dispute has spilled well beyond trade. Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st US state, ordered US federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America" and continued to attack Canadian leaders online.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

US officials have also mocked Canada's military, prompting Carney to accuse Washington of "doing memes", "throwing shade" and "trying to be tough".

But beneath the memes and insults is a serious economic standoff that both sides still say could ultimately be resolved at the negotiating table.

Origins of the feud

While Trump has imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion ($27 billion) worth of Canadian goods, Canada is preparing retaliatory tariffs of roughly the same value on US products from 8 September.

But the disagreement isn't just about tariffs.

Carney says the US was seeking terms that would have left major Canadian industries, particularly the highly integrated auto sector, effectively operating as subsidiaries of US companies.

He has also accused the US of seeking changes that would affect Canada's French-language and cultural protections, as well as restrictions on Canada's ability to negotiate future free trade agreements with other countries.

Canada has rejected those demands as a threat to its economic interests and sovereignty.

The Trump administration disputes Canada's account of the negotiations and has argued that a deal was available that Canada chose not to accept.

Why has sovereignty become such a big issue?

Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st US state, a proposal Canada has firmly rejected.

What might once have sounded like political provocation has become a central part of the dispute, with Carney increasingly framing the confrontation as a defence of Canadian sovereignty.

That rhetoric carries particular weight in Quebec, where there are concerns about what US absorption of Canada could mean for the province's French language and culture.

Carney has also pushed back against any suggestion that the US should have a say over who Canada trades with.

"Canada is a sovereign state," he said.

"We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals with."

Why is the rhetoric getting so personal?

Since the trade talks collapsed, Trump has repeatedly attacked Canada's leadership and used social media to taunt the country.

He has described Canada's leaders as among the worst he has to deal with, and posted an AI-generated meme depicting Canadian geese with his distinctive hairstyle marching under a US flag.

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth appeared to take aim at Canada's military, posting an image of two female Canadian military cadets training in British Columbia with the words "this is real" alongside a Canadian flag.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent also mocked Canada's military, later saying that Carney had received a "verbal beatdown" from him and Hegseth.

Carney said the comments from members of Trump's administration were "beneath their office".

"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions," Carney said.

Why does it matter beyond the insults?

The US and Canada have one of the world's most deeply integrated economic relationships.

That means prolonged disruption could affect workers, businesses and consumers on both sides of the border, particularly in industries such as manufacturing and autos, where supply chains frequently cross the border.

The Canadian government has warned that it cannot accept an agreement that it believes would weaken its domestic industries or limit its ability to make its own economic decisions.

At the same time, Carney has stressed that Canada is not looking for a permanent economic rupture with its largest trading partner.

On Thursday, he said Canada was ready to sign a deal with the US if it benefited both countries and provided "stability and credibility".

He also suggested there had been a recent softening in Washington's position.

Carney said the US had been pushing certain demands around Canadian language and culture right up until the talks collapsed, but was no longer insisting on them.

"Now, they're not," he said. "Well, if they didn't care, they shouldn't have kept them in the deal."

Is a deal still possible?

Despite the increasingly bitter rhetoric, Carney says the door to negotiations remains open.

He has repeatedly said Canada is prepared to return to the table when the US is ready to have serious discussions.

Trump's response has been less conciliatory.

After Carney's comments on Thursday, Trump posted that it was "very good for Canadian Politicians like Prime Minister Mark Carney to make President Donald J. Trump 'the enemy.'"

He warned that Canada's economy could collapse and be "worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian politician".

So while the memes, insults and threats have grabbed the headlines, the underlying dispute remains fundamentally about power.

Canada is trying to protect its industries and preserve its ability to make independent economic and cultural decisions.

Trump's administration is pushing for a trade relationship on terms more favourable to the US.

And both sides are now testing how far they are willing to go, without completely severing a relationship that neither country can easily walk away from.

title: Argentine president reignites Falklands dispute after Trump questions UK sovereignty
text:
In brief Argentine President Javier Milei has reignited a dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands.

It comes after US President Donald Trump said the US would reconsider its neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty.

Argentine President Javier Milei escalated his country's long-running dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, praising US President Donald Trump for saying the US could reconsider its historically neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty.

In a nationally televised address on Thursday night local time, Milei seized on Trump's comments this week that the US could review its position on the islands, casting the potential shift as proof that his close relationship with the US president — often criticised by political opponents — was paying dividends.

"The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come," Milei said.

The libertarian Argentine leader then announced a series of actions aimed at stopping the development of the Sea Lion oil project, about 220km north of the islands, where UK company Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum plan to begin drilling in the coming months and start producing oil in 2028.

Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.

He threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in offshore drilling and announced new funding for a naval base in Argentina's southernmost province, Tierra del Fuego, to bolster the country's military presence near the islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

"Argentina will not stand idly by," Milei said. "Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security."

READ MORE Argentina faces FIFA fine after players celebrate win against England with Falklands banner

Milei's effort to refocus national attention on the Falklands marks a striking turn for a leader who has faced criticism at home for warming ties with the UK and professing admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the UK prime minister who led the country to retake the remote archipelago during the 1982 Falklands War after Argentina had invaded it.

The two-month conflict killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders.

The sovereignty claim remains one of the few causes that cuts across Argentina's stark political divides, giving Milei a welcome political opening as his approval ratings slip and the economy sputters.

"We can argue about my style. We can disagree over fiscal or exchange-rate policy," Milei said.

"But this issue demands that we lay down our arms and show a united front to the world as a nation and as a society. There are causes that rise above any political difference. The Malvinas is one of them."

Argentina maintains that it inherited sovereignty over the islands from its former coloniser, Spain, and that the UK has illegally occupied them since 1833. The UK rejects that claim, citing the islanders' desire to remain a British overseas territory.

Britain insisted that the Falkland Islands "are British" after Milei's comments.

"The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British," British defence secretary Wes Streeting responded in a social media post on Friday.

"Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable," Streeting added.

Trump questions US support for British sovereignty

For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing Argentine and UK sovereignty claims over the Falklands while recognising the UK's de facto administration of the islands. Any departure from that position would be a major diplomatic affront and inflame already high trans-Atlantic tensions.

On Monday, Trump fuelled frenzied speculation in the UK when asked whether his administration was reviewing its stance on the decades-old dispute.

"I always review every position," he replied. "That's just one of many."

Then, in an interview aired on Thursday with UK broadcaster GB News, Trump avoided directly answering a question about whether the US would "come to the aid" of the UK in another conflict over the Falklands.

The Falkland Islands have been under UK control for nearly 200 years. Credit: Supplied

Instead, he repeated past complaints that Britain had not provided sufficient support for the US-led bombing campaign against Iran.

"Your country was not there to help me," Trump said, recalling that the UK's former prime minister, Keir Starmer, told him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign.

"It was pretty sad, the whole thing."

The Trump administration has floated the Falklands as leverage before: An internal Pentagon email leaked in April first raised the prospect of the US reconsidering its position on the islands as one possible way to punish NATO allies that declined to join the US war on Iran.

In response, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman, Tom Wells, said the British government's position was "long-standing and unwavering".

"Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount," Wells said earlier this week, pointing to a 2013 referendum in which the roughly 4,000 people living in the Falkland Islands voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a British overseas territory.
