title: Phase two of the Kiss-era Wallabies is about to begin. There is one lingering concern
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Phase two of the Kiss-era Wallabies is about to begin. There is one lingering concern Iain Payten September 6, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Peering into a laptop during a virtual press conference after a win over Argentina on Sunday morning, Wallabies coach Les Kiss was explaining why he’d been so persistently funky with selections - and substitutions - during his first five weeks in charge. In a run of four Tests against Japan and Argentina, Kiss made an average of eight changes to his starting team for each game. And then when games were underway, the coach responded to injuries and substitutions by sometimes rearranging several positions at a time. Loading “There’s a combination we’ve never seen before - or will see again,” Stan commentator Sean Maloney said when looking at a backline of Kalani Thomas, Ryan Lonergan, Len Ikitau, Isaac Henry and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii. Injuries informed some of that jigsaw - and we learned Lonergan is a tidy No.10 - but Kiss said there was a method to the madness.

Advertisement

“Some of the things we’re trying to work on is to make ourselves a bit future-proof,” Kiss said. “So we become adaptable in those spaces.” There was a risk to Kiss’ strategy. Changing half of the team each week could have exposed the team to a lack of cohesion against sides with proven capacity to beat big nations. Les Kiss poses with the Wallabies in a team photo ahead of the Mendoza Test. Getty Images And things definitely spluttered at times, but not enough to bring on disaster. Three wins and a draw from four Tests is no small feat, and there is credit due, particularly to the forwards, who have swiftly become the centre of the Wallabies’ game. There also needs to appreciate the difficulty of doing it all mostly on the road - particularly in Argentina.

Advertisement

As he did ahead of the Mendoza Test, Kiss also indicated to the laptop that the time had come for the experimentation phase to end, and the start of a more settled team phase to start. There is just over one year until the 2027 Rugby World Cup, and history tells us World Cup winners are usually playing together in a discernible combination in the year prior. Loading “I was just talking to the coaches earlier. We feel that some of the decisions we’ve made over these four or five weeks, we got a lot of good information from it,” Kiss said. “That’ll certainly narrow the mindset in terms of how we go forward for sure. It was important that this whole group knew we were going to back them. They knew that we were going to challenge them in many different ways ... we’ll get a lot of pay from that down the road.”

Advertisement

Next up is a clash with the Springboks in Perth on September 27. The Boks will be coming out of the four-Test series against the All Blacks battered, but also battle-hardened. Kiss has some tough calls to make about who makes his discernible combination. There are surplus options in the back row, front row and centres. That depth is a bonus. More worryingly, the back three has become a mess, with only Max Jorgensen a certain pick. Len Ikitau of Australia takes on Faustino Sanchez Valarolo of Argentina. Getty Images Perhaps the most concerning part for Kiss and the Wallabies, in both the form seen in the four Tests and the selection picture for the future, is the wobbly game management from the halves and fullback. The Wallabies have at times looked unstoppable with the ball, when rolling downhill in the rival half. The power and pace of forward runners, via Lonergan’s sharp service, is on par with any side in the world.

Advertisement

But the Wallabies have also struggled to play with composure when on the back foot, and be smart and efficient when exiting their own half. Time and again, errors in getting to a good kick and playing down the other end have resulted in the Wallabies putting themselves under pressure. Worryingly, those errors even came in batches. Pablo Matera’s second, go-ahead try in Mendoza came after four botched exits in a row. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii in action against Argentina. Getty Images No matter how good your defence or your ability to win turnovers, the modern game is now like the NFL: if you spend too much time in your half, you’ll concede points. Tom Wright’s chronic impulsiveness from fullback is also manna from heaven for rivals hoping for unearned access to the red zone.

Advertisement

“The problem is at times we’re probably not just managing the game away from our third of the pitch enough times,” Kiss said. “We’re just probably three steps forward in controlling the game and then suddenly one or two steps (back), we’re back on our back foot again.” Related Article Opinion

Wallabies Les Kiss knows his strongest Wallabies side. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author The problem Kiss faces is that the simple solution - picking the best game manager - could be off the table for the Boks’ clash. Carter Gordon has shown himself to be the most reliable option for steering the Wallabies around. But at the ground where one of his mentors, Quade Cooper, suffered a ruptured Achilles tendon in 2022, Gordon hobbled off with an ankle injury and went for scans. That’s usually a precursor to bad news, meaning Kiss may need to turn back to Declan Meredith or Ben Donaldson to be the game manager to meet the Springboks.

Advertisement

After five weeks under Les Kiss, the Wallabies have shown they have depth, forward power, a mostly strong set piece, and the belief to defend for long periods and win turnovers. They’ve also shown they have the tendency to shoot themselves in the foot. When you’re playing South Africa and New Zealand, you can’t give them any help.

title: Farage says Britain is broken and only Reform can fix it. Now the pressure is on to deliver
text:
Nigel Farage, in the party’s trademark light blue, is under pressure in parliament and the media. He’ll also have to address the palpable frustration among ordinary people about the state of their communities.

From a distance, it is easy to dismiss Reform as an extreme movement that wants to overturn British politics with radical change. Up close, however, the members are ordinary people with everyday concerns.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Birmingham: A feudal king is striding through the crowd as thousands of Reform UK members gather to hear their leader, Nigel Farage, remind them that they are on a mission to save Britain. The king is dressed in faux chain mail, a crown and a red cloak embroidered with lions – a reminder of the country’s glorious past. And he is an instant hit with the Reform faithful. Chris Luck has come to the annual Reform conference dressed as Richard the Lionheart, famous for defending English territory and waging crusades against Muslim enemies. Luck, 62, enjoys medieval re-enactments when he is not working in the distribution business from his home in Bracknell, west of London. His reason for wearing this outfit today, he says, is to remind Britain what makes it great. “The main problem with this country is immigration,” he tells me. “That’s the thing that needs to get sorted out. And once they get that sorted out, that’s going to affect everything else that’s wrong with the country, because all the money is being wasted on them.” Chris Luck says he dressed as Richard the Lionheart to remind Britain what makes it great. David Crowe By them, he means migrants. He wants a complete stop to unauthorised arrivals. He believes the government has set up an “invitation machine” by offering too many welfare and housing incentives for asylum seekers who come by boat across the English Channel. And he blames Labour and the Conservative Party: “They’re all traitors.” There is plenty of passion for the Reform movement here in this vast conference hall on the edge of Birmingham, where party members are spending two or three days to see the leaders they admire. Some are enjoying some political cosplay by dressing up, especially in the party’s trademark light blue, but most look like the people you see on an average English high street. Whatever they are wearing, they share Luck’s concern about migration. From a distance, it is easy to dismiss Reform as an extreme movement that wants to overturn British politics with radical change. Up close, however, the members are ordinary people with everyday concerns. And that is exactly why the party remains so significant even when Farage is tainted by scandals over donations from wealthy crypto investors and the sudden resignation of two aides caught on camera talking about taking money from foreign donors.

Advertisement

Farage is under pressure in the parliament and the media, but that’s not the only pressure that counts. A much more powerful force, over time, is the palpable frustration among ordinary people about the state of their communities. As society changes, tension grows. And people will demand to be heard. Susan Morrell, a small business owner, was a member of the Liberal Democrats, the UK’s middle-of the-road party, for 32 years. She served on the local council in her town of Coalville, in the English Midlands, and supported Labour at times, but she has joined Reform because she worries about the degradation of government services. She believes migration is a key problem. “It’s overwhelming the country and we’ve got to be realistic about it,” she says. Susan Morrell, who believes migration is a key problem, in front of a poster of Farage urging members to consider standing for election for the party. David Crowe Morrell is the daughter of a migrant who came to England from Austria in the 1950s. She is not against migration, but she is worried about the scale of the influx in recent times when she sees the change in the nearby city of Leicester. “I’ve always been kind of in the centre of politics, but I’ve moved a little bit more to the centre right,” she says. “I’ve seen how Leicester has changed over the last 10 years. There are an awful lot of people that just hang around, and they’ve obviously not got anything particular to do, and they’ve not come in on work visas. They’ve not gone the proper route.” When Morrell’s father required medical help last month, she struggled to get what he needed. He was sent home without a care package, she says, even though he had broken his sternum and ribs. When she broke her foot in June, she says, she was sent home from the medical walk-in centre and had to drive herself in pain.

Advertisement

“I’m thinking, well, this is just not right. You don’t know it until you experience it, what’s happening on the front line. And it’s not that the staff are awful people, it’s just that they’re overwhelmed. “I think that’s what’s really, really done it. It’s the sheer numbers for me.” In Britain, as in Australia, hospitals and aged-care homes depend heavily on workers from overseas. Of the 1.5 million workers in the National Health Service, around 325,000 were born overseas, according to the House of Commons Library. That represents about one in five health workers. (The biggest source countries are India, the Philippines, Nigeria, Ireland and Poland). Loading The challenge for Britain, and the source of frustration for Reform members, is that life does not seem to be improving as a result of migration. Whether the complaints are about healthcare, or drug addicts on the high street, or rubbish in the alleyways or slow progress on building new roads, there is an overwhelming sense of decline in living standards. One of the most effective refrains from Farage captures this sense of gloom. “Nothing works any more in this country,” he says. Another refrain tells voters he is their only hope. “Britain is broken: only Reform can fix it.” Vicky Shaw, a nurse, is loud and proud at the Reform conference in Birmingham. She arrives in a light blue jacket, with a matching cowboy hat in the party colours, and she has good reason to be confident about the party’s future. She was elected as a councillor on the Crewe Town Council in May, when Reform confirmed its rise by defeating Labour and the Conservatives in many neighbourhoods.

Advertisement

Shaw says health services are under severe stress and migration has not helped, even though it has brought in some workers. “The way it’s working at the moment, there’s too many managerial roles and not enough nurses,” she says. In her view, government money is being wasted in other areas when health needs more support, and she believes the passage of asylum seekers across the English Channel has to end. “I think we should stop the boats,” she says. “I think that any government that allows it to happen has blood on their hands for every death in the channel. They could easily stop the boats – get the army, get the navy to stop them.” Vicky Shaw says health services are under severe stress and migration has not helped. David Crowe The boat arrivals make headlines every time dozens of migrants make it on to an inflatable dinghy from the beaches of France and Belgium, but the numbers vary. There were no arrivals in the week to September 4. In the final week of August, however, 616 migrants arrived on 10 boats. The rolling tally at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford shows the annual rate has fallen to about 32,000. This is down from last year but is about three times the inflow seen in 2021. The argument in Britain mirrors the years of dispute in Australia about whether asylum seekers are motivated by “push” factors from their home countries or the “pull” factors about living in London or other cities. One thing that grates on voters is that asylum seekers are often housed during processing in hotels in residential neighbourhoods, giving them a quality of accommodation beyond the budgets of most people. Steve Trevelyan, a former soldier who lives in St Austell in Cornwall, thinks the asylum seekers are responding to a signal sent out by the British government.

Advertisement

“I can’t blame them. Our governments give them an incentive to come over – housing, money, mobile phones, they put them up in five-star hotels. But you’ve got veterans on the streets who don’t get that,” he says. What is the solution? “Don’t offer these incentives. People will go to wherever they get handouts. If there are genuine cases where there are asylum or persecution, possibly [let them in]. But we do know the majority are coming over for the economic benefits.” Labour and the Conservatives have been wary of shutting down assistance for asylum seekers, given decades of support for refugees under British law. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, would face a backlash from his Labour party room if he attempted to remove benefits, but there is a live debate in Britain about whether the current law makes it too hard for border authorities to remove migrants. One factor is that migrants contesting their removal can rely on the European Convention on Human Rights, an international treaty the UK supports. This has totemic importance for Reform, which describes the ECHR as a sign of weak national government. Farage vows to remove the UK from the treaty and make sure judges have to order more asylum seekers out of the country. On the conference floor in Birmingham, Reform members name the ECHR as a key issue. But it is not the only issue. Trevelyan names “woke” politics from progressive causes, free speech and welfare as some of his concerns. We speak after he has just signed a condolence book to express grief at the death of Ann Widdecombe, the former Conservative and Reform politician who was killed in her home in July. Widdecombe made enemies with her traditional social values, especially when she argued against activists for trans rights. A man has been charged with her murder. Farage is scrambling to control the political damage from the donation scandal hanging over him and his party. On Friday morning, hours before he addressed the party conference in Birmingham, he removed the two aides caught on camera talking about funding from overseas donors, which is banned under donations law. He says the aides were suspended for “loose pub talk” but insists he and the party have done nothing wrong.

title: ‘Caught in a trap’: The most expensive regions for insurance on Australia’s east coast revealed
text:
Megan Vicary lives where the Nepean meets the Hawkesbury River, and across the road from the Grose River.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Across the country, Australia is falling behind in adapting to the baked-in impacts of climate change. See all stories .

Megan Vicary is among the growing ranks of Australians who do not carry full home insurance. The 52-year-old moved to her 10-hectare property in Yarramundi in the Hawkesbury region nine years ago and had an insurance policy that cost her about $6000 a year. After four floods in 2022, it went up to $35,000 a year, and she could no longer justify the expense. Now, the quotes are as high as $50,000 a year, and many insurers won’t offer flood coverage at all, based on her postcode. She still has a policy, but it doesn’t cover flood. “No one’s insuring for flood,” Vicary says. “If we have a major flood, it is going to be a crisis because none of us can afford it. All the way down the riverbank, none of us are flood-covered.” The same crisis is playing out nationally as mounting climate disasters drive up insurance risk, and consumers drop their coverage, preferring to self insure or hope for a government bailout. As the United Nations reports that the goal of curbing global warming to 1.5 degrees has failed, the task of climate adaptation grows more important. Insurance is at the heart of the challenge. Across Australia, the regions with the highest insurance premiums are those with the most flood risk, and this is particularly true on the east coast, according to analysis prepared exclusively for this masthead by actuarial firm Finity. Bushfires are a factor, too, but flood is the overwhelming driver.

Advertisement

The most expensive insurance on the east coast is in the Richmond-Tweed region in the NSW Northern Rivers, when comparing large sub-state regions defined by the Australian Bureau of Statistics as statistical area 4 (SA4). In Richmond-Tweed, near the Queensland border, premiums have risen 81 per cent since January 2021. The average quote for a new policy in the region, which includes Lismore, Tweed Heads, Murwillumbah, Byron Bay and Ballina, is now $8836 a year. The most expensive insurance in Victoria by SA4 is in the Shepparton region, where the average quote is $4871 a year, up 77 per cent. The highest in Queensland is in the west of Brisbane, where home owners now pay an average of $6173, up 74 per cent. What all three regions have in common is that they were hit by devastating floods, sometimes numerous times, over the past decade, and most especially in 2022. NSW premiums are particularly high because they include the emergency services levy of between 15 and 18 per cent, which is not funded through insurance in other states. The NSW government is considering reforms. Premiums in the Cairns SA4 region have gone down over the past five years and are now an average $3985 a year. Finity principal Stephen Lau says this is because the federal government created a cyclone reinsurance pool in northern Australia to make insurance more affordable in cyclone-prone areas. The program is monitored by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

Advertisement

In some locations, it is possible to zoom in even closer to clusters of individual suburbs. Breaking down the Blue Mountains and Outer West sub-state region into three SA3 sub-regions reveals that the Richmond-Windsor area – where Yarramundi is located – has average premiums of $12,606 a year, a rise of 91 per cent over five years. Again, the main reason is flood risk. But in Victoria, the most expensive of these smaller regions is the Yarra Ranges, east of Melbourne, which has an average premium of $5183 a year, an 81 per cent rise mainly because of fire risk. Related Article Climate crisis ‘The homes we build twice’: Repair bill for climate disasters climbing faster than inflation Analysis used by the Insurance Council of Australia suggests the most vulnerable people and communities in Australia have the highest flood risk but the lowest financial and social capacity to protect their properties and families and to recover from disaster. Council chief executive Andrew Hall is hugely concerned by this trend. “When the worst happens to them, and most of the time I’m talking flooding, they just go backwards, and [that] creates this intergenerational cycle of poverty because they’re caught in a trap that they can’t get out of,” Hall says. “They can’t sell their home [because] no one buys it back. It gets rebuilt in the location it was in, or they’ve just got no money and they’re stuck trying to put together what they’ve got left. That is the big picture.”

Advertisement

About 1.4 million properties nationally face some risk of flooding, including almost 300,000 properties that face a severe-to-extreme annual flooding risk, largely in NSW, Queensland and Victoria, the Insurance Council says. The cost of dealing with natural disasters without insurance is high. Megan Vicary’s home was built nine years ago, and comprehensive insurance with flood cover now costs about $50,000 a year. Wolter Peeters Vicary’s home was built in the past nine years and sits about five metres above what is commonly referred to as the one-in-100-year flood line – though more accurately, that means there is a 1 per cent chance of flooding in any given year. The water has never risen as high as her house, but the clean-up is still a big task. Related Article Climate crisis ‘Little by little cities will have to recede’: Coastal flooding is the sleeper climate issue “Even if you don’t get floodwater in your home, when that river comes up, you’ve got all the animals that come out of everywhere – the mice, the snakes, the bugs,” Vicary says. “Mildew starts to grow in your house – I literally for weeks had to turn my air-conditioner on to get the humidity out of my house, so I didn’t have mould growing.” Her lower paddocks front the river, so she has to evacuate animals – including alpacas, sheep and horses – and then clean up for their safe return. She has spent $65,000 of her savings on replacing fences, cleaning out low-lying sheds and disposing of the debris dumped by the river, including a washing machine and half a speedboat.

Advertisement

Australia remains a relatively well-insured nation, but the protection gap is growing. The Insurance Council’s Alix Pearce wrote in a Churchill fellowship report titled Insuring Australia Tomorrow in January that, of Australia’s $US37 billion ($51.7 billion) in losses from extreme weather over the past decade, $US12 billion, or about a third, was not insured. Between 1987 and 2015, the number of properties exposed to high flood risk increased by more than 65 per cent both because of more homes being built and also climate change increasing the physical risk. The average cost to build a new house in Australia has risen by 30 per cent since 2021, faster than the cumulative inflation rate of 24 per cent over the same time frame, the Insurance Council reported this week. When damaged properties are repaired under insurance, they are held to outdated building standards, which means they will not be resilient to worsening weather. People who can afford it are taking matters into their own hands and disaster-proofing their homes. Bec Nicoll and Sarah Thomson at their nearly completed resilient home in Kialla, near Shepparton. Justin McManus Building back better Sarah Thomson, 53, and Bec Nicoll, 56, moved into their newly rebuilt home in Kialla, near Shepparton, a week ago, more than four years after they were flooded by Seven Creeks, a tributary of the Murray.

Advertisement

They are relieved and delighted, after first living in a caravan for nine months and then in a 36-square-metre shed for more than three years. They have built back better, putting in about $500,000 of their own money on top of the insurance payout. First, they had to battle with their insurance company, Allianz, for 12 months to be allowed to demolish and rebuild. “They said that it was repairable, but the slab was still wet after nearly 12 months, and we didn’t want to be putting floorboards on top of a wet slab,” Thomson says. “Negotiating with the insurer was a long, tedious, irritating process. That’s not available to a lot of people. We’ve got the ability to actually negotiate and to be able to fight for a good outcome.” Nicoll says Emergency Recovery Victoria provided teams of engineers and hygienists who recommended demolition, but Allianz “completely disregarded” the report as too generic. Eventually, the couple engaged a private engineer and researched insurance law to force the issue. Allianz chief claims officer Luke Whenman apologised if Thomson and Nicoll had had a bad experience. He said the company always looked for the best way to build back within the funding envelope, and that it could provide an extra $20,000 to boost resilience. Cash settlement was not a good option for most customers because they would be unable to find tradespeople after a disaster, he said. Sarah Thomson and Bec Nicoll spent nine months living in a caravan and more than three years in their shed. Just in McManus Thomson and Nicoll’s new house is raised on stumps and is also on a hillside, making it 1.25 metres higher than their old home and above the one-in-100-year flood level, with a buffer for climate change. They have also adhered to Passivhaus principles for temperature control and relevant bushfire codes. None of this has made a difference to their new insurance premiums. Before the flood, they were paying between $2000 and $2500. They have now found insurance for $6100 a year, having fielded some quotes as high as $18,000 a year. When shopping around, the couple found there was nowhere to disclose any of the resilience features of their new home. “When I said to a sales agent that we’ve actually rebuilt well above the mandated height for flooding in our area, he said, ‘that’s nice, I’m happy for you, but that doesn’t alter the policy’,” Nicoll says. It was a similar story for home owners in northern NSW who flood-proofed their dwellings after being inundated in 2022. Virginia Jones and her husband, Tim Lawson, in Bogangar, near Cabarita Beach, put their home on stilts, raising it so high that a full-size netball hoop stand could fit underneath. Their next-door neighbour Bernie Zietlow rebuilt his home with materials that mean it could be hosed out after a flood. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster Jones says her insurance premiums have more than doubled to about $6000 a year, despite the lower flood risk because of raising the property. Zietlow’s insurance premiums have gone up from $1000 to $4000 a year for a small home. He has priced insurance with and without the improvements, and it made no difference. This is a problem that the Housing Resilience Action Plan aims to solve. A collaboration between Finity, the Resilient Building Council, Monash University and consumer advocacy groups, the proposal is to develop a rating system for every home in Australia that insurers use when pricing premiums. Finity principal Sharanjit Paddam says the rating for each type of natural disaster would incorporate the risk profile of the area and the resilience of the actual home. “The idea … is to have a common language, so that consumers understand what the resilience of their home is to different disasters, insurers use that information to price insurance contracts, and then banks lend people money so that they can get the house to a different resilience level,” Paddam says. “When you get your renewal notice, they’ll say, ‘OK, you are three-star-rated against flood, and that has led to this pricing for your insurance premium, but if you were four-star-rated, this is what your premium would be’. Including signals like that can empower consumers to make decisions.” Lowering community risk Related Article Analysis

Climate policy The world made a ‘covenant with the future’ – and we broke it Scott Hawkins, managing director for Australasia at global reinsurance company Munich RE, says lowering the risk of events that occur every three to five years won’t significantly reduce premiums. It’s mitigating the risk of more extreme events that occur every few decades that would make the difference, he says. “Some things people can do at the home level, but some things need to be done at the community level,” Hawkins says. The Insurance Council has called for a 10-year, $30 billion flood defence fund to bolster infrastructure in 24 priority catchments nationally. The catchments were chosen because of flood risk and insurance affordability pressure. They are all in the eastern states. Hall says the government has the right idea with the Hazards Insurance Partnership, which is designed to fund community and household infrastructure that can reduce risk and put downward pressure on premiums. That is world-leading, Hall says, because the government persuaded insurance companies to provide information into the program, whereas in other developed jurisdictions such as the United States, governments had to sue to get access to the commercially sensitive data. Related Article Electricity Bruce’s home was ‘like a tent’. A new energy rating is guiding upgrades The government also created the Disaster Ready Fund, which was $200 million a year, though it has recently been reduced to $142.4 million. “Again, huge tick, very smart idea,” Hall says. “The problem with it is that … so far… they’re programs like teaching people about bushfire awareness or building cyclone shelters.” Hall says there would be more downward pressure on premiums if the money were spent on hard infrastructure and community-level defences, such as flood levees. NationalQueenslandBrisbane development Luxury riverside towers to be built at former athletes village site Julius Dennis September 6, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Luxury towers expected to house up to 5000 people will be erected on a riverside block previously slated for the Olympic athletes village in Hamilton. Deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie announced the project, that will be handled by five separate developers, on Sunday – the latest in his spree of announcements about the sell-off of underutilised state-owned land. The six-hectare block will be split between five separate developers, with the 13 towers expected to deliver 2200 apartments ranging from one to four bedrooms. The towers will be delivered by five developers. Queensland state government A shopping centre, hotel, childcare facility and medical services will also be built as part of the development between Wharf and Theodore streets.

Advertisement

Towers closer to the water will be built by Red & Co, Joe Adsett Developments and Graya, while those further back will be developed by Lancini and Greyburn. All three of the riverfront towers will contain housing and retail spaces, with the Graya building to also have a 50-bed hotel. The block has long been eyed off by developers. Julius Dennis The Lancini building will be the centre of the development, with a 15,000-square-metre shopping centre with a supermarket and space for potential medical, child care and educational services. Greyburn will develop four medium-height complexes with ground floor retail.

Advertisement

The state will spend $154 million over the next year-and-a-half on road upgrades and preparing the sites, with work expected to begin in 2028. The Red & Co site. Queensland state government Bleijie said Wharf Street would be extended to stretch further along the water, with community lawns and shade, with renders showing walking and bike infrastructure along the river. BusinessMarketsBillionaires Opinion Billionaire’s $6.3m ‘bride price’ stunt could backfire

Shuli Ren September 6, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just when Bitcoin seemed to be breaking out of its long winter, a publicity stunt by one of the crypto industry’s most prominent billionaires is raising questions as to whether this asset class should be in mainstream investors’ portfolios. Justin Sun, the Trump family’s earliest and biggest crypto backer, is suing a Chinese actress and her parents to recover what he describes as a bride price of 30 million yuan ($6.3 million). In a long essay posted on X, titled “My Girlfriend Jing Tian,” he recounts their relationship and portrays Jing as high-maintenance and money-hungry. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun has come under heavy fire for his latest stunt. Bloomberg This dispute has captivated Chinese society and the crypto world. The original August 27 X post alone has garnered 40 million views. In response, Jing wrote on Chinese social media Weibo, where she has more than 26 million followers, that she would never trade love for money and believes that justice would prevail. With an estimated net worth of $US8.3 billion, Sun is an expert in creating media buzz, sometimes as a way to boost the value of his business dealings. He is known for spending $US6.2 million at Sotheby’s on a conceptual artwork composed of a fresh banana stuck to a wall — and eating it in front of reporters afterwards.

Advertisement

The crypto billionaire is also litigious, suing World Liberty Financial, a crypto project co-founded by President Donald Trump, for extortion after their business associations turned sour. The company counter-sued for defamation. He also previously sued Bloomberg for reporting on his wealth, but ultimately voluntarily dismissed his case. But is this publicity stunt smart? Flamboyance doesn’t bode well when the Chinese government embraces common prosperity and is keen to rein in capital flight. In the well-crafted essay — the 36-year-old won a national writing competition in 2007 that secured him a spot at the prestigious Peking University — Sun spent pages flaunting his wealth. He’s especially fond of his Airbus A330, estimated to be worth $US200 million, boasting that the Maldives airport is too small for the private plane and the islanders at Tenerife off West Africa had never seen anything like it. Chinese actress Tian Jing has appeared in films such as 2017’s Kong: Skull Island. AP The public backlash in China was almost immediate, with prominent influencers calling Sun vengeful and a social outcast (crypto trading is illegal in China). Over the weekend, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who was instrumental in Sun’s early success, suggested he tone down the rhetoric.

Advertisement

After all, we don’t need to look far to see how Beijing feels about flashy displays of wealth. In 2022, regulators asked the entire brokerage industry to implement pay cuts after the wife of a junior trader at China International Capital Corp. drew public ire by revealing her husband’s monthly salary on social media. Finance executives’ compensation only started to bottom out last year. China more recently has been cracking down on capital flight, banning unauthorised offshore issuance of yuan-pegged stablecoins. These cryptocurrencies allow people to move money internationally without sharing identifying information, even bypassing stringent economic sanctions. View post on X It’s not hard to see how Sun may irritate Beijing. The bulk of his wealth stems from Tron, a blockchain system that has morphed into a global payments network that moves much more than PayPal. Nearly 40 per cent of Tether’s USDT, the world’s most-used dollar-pegged stablecoin, is transacted on Tron, which counted Asian crime syndicates among its early adopters, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Meanwhile, crypto exchange HTX, where Sun is a self-described advisor, hosts plenty of suspicious activities. It has been accused by the UK and the European Union of helping Russia move money. HTX has pushed back, saying Huobi Global SA — the first defendant in a legal claim the UK has made — is distinct from the online exchange, which is committed to full compliance worldwide.

Advertisement

At last week’s Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, Binance’s Zhao tried to strike a bullish tone, predicting that Bitcoin will soon overtake gold. But there are plenty of sceptics. Both assets are floated as potential beneficiaries of the so-called debasement trade — whereby investors seek refuge from the dollar for fear that it’s being devalued — but legally they’re miles apart. Central banks are buying gold to diversify their reserves, while the crypto industry still operates in a tight regulatory environment and as such, it can ill afford negative coverage now. Unfortunately, Sun’s sordid essay will deepen the public’s crypto scepticism and fatigue. Related Article Crime ‘Heinous’ crime: China’s disgraced king of real estate sentenced to life in jail

title: How backyard mozzie traps curbed the spread of a flesh-eating disease in Melbourne suburbia
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive NationalVictoriaHealthcare How backyard mozzie traps curbed the spread of a flesh-eating disease in Melbourne suburbia Melissa Cunningham September 6, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first, it looked like an innocuous insect bite on the top of Sarah Fowler’s foot. The 52-year-old Brunswick woman noticed the small raised bump while staying with her parents on the Mornington Peninsula on New Year’s Day last year. Sarah Fowler was diagnosed with a Buruli ulcer last year after being bitten by an infected mosquito months earlier in Brunswick West. Joe Armao She went to a GP who prescribed her antibiotics. But the bump kept growing until it looked like a golf ball and her foot began to swell and ache. Weeks later, a doctor at hospital emergency department diagnosed her with a flesh-eating Buruli ulcer.

Advertisement

Related Article Graphic content

Good Weekend Stigma, isolation: the flesh-eating ulcer infecting hundreds more Victorians each year Last year, Victoria reported a record-breaking 426 cases of the tissue-destroying ulcer, and more than 100 infections have already been reported this year. As the state heads into the riskiest months for transmission, the landmark findings of a study from a group of researchers at The Doherty Institute and University of Melbourne could change how Australia halts the spread of the flesh-eating bacteria. As part of a world-first trial, researchers set up almost 600 specialised eco-friendly mosquito control traps, known as auto-dissemination stations, across transmission hotspots in the Merri-bek and Moonee Valley council areas targeting suburbs in the north-west including Brunswick West, Essendon and Moonee Ponds. Scientists have long believed mosquitoes are fuelling the spread of the mysterious disease by biting infected possums and then humans.

Advertisement

The skin infection is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium ulcerans. If it gets under the skin, it can grow and produce a toxin that can melt skin cells and fat. One of the lead researchers, University of Melbourne medical entomologist Dr Véronique Paris, said control stations were set up in residents’ backyards and in suburban streets to target mosquitoes breeding in small, hidden sources of water around people’s homes. Dr Véronique Paris and fellow researcher Dr Andrew Buultjens helped lead a world-first trial to halt the spread of the flesh-eating Buruli ulcer. Simon Schluter The black plastic container traps used scent and water to lure in female mosquitoes before coating them in a slow-acting larvicide powder. The insects then unwittingly carried the toxin to surrounding water sources, which could be anywhere from a neighbour’s water tank to roof gutters, killing off mosquito larvae across the entire neighbourhood. Paris said after eight weeks, between January and March 2024, mosquito egg counts plummeted by about 70 per cent in areas with the traps, effectively suppressing the entire insect population.

Advertisement

“But what surprised us most was the actual impact on the human cases of Buruli ulcer,” Paris said. Related Article Healthcare The unusual vaccination plan to halt ‘out of control’ flesh-eating disease After the trial, researchers compared Buruli ulcer cases reported in the six protected zones, which were fitted with the traps, against six nearby untouched “control areas” to measure how well the mosquito stations prevented human infections. Paris said it was a complex task given it can take many months for Buruli ulcers to develop in the skin after a person is bitten. Their analysis showed that residents in areas with traps were 83 per cent less likely to contract Buruli ulcers than those in unprotected zones.

Advertisement

Professor Tim Stinear, director of the World Health Organisation Collaborating Centre for Mycobacterium ulcerans at the Doherty Institute, said the findings, published in the Nature Microbiology scientific journal, showed for the first time that reducing mosquito populations could significantly reduce the risk of infection in people. Related Article Illness Flesh-eating ulcer ‘endemic’ in coastal town with ‘significant risk’ of spread to Sydney The microbiologist at the University of Melbourne said the study showed the traps were not only effective at controlling mosquitoes where the control stations were located, but also in surrounding areas. “We don’t have to kill all mosquitoes, that’s not the message,” Stinear said. “But this trial shows if we can reduce mozzie numbers by simple control measures, then we can measurably reduce transmission risk of the disease.” Stinear said even adopting simple mosquito control measures at a community level, such as using insect repellent, covering water tanks, installing fly screens and eliminating breeding sites around the home, could reduce the risk of infection.

Advertisement

Sarah Fowler was shocked to discover she had been bitten by a mosquito months before the strange bite even appeared, while she was living in the hotspot of Brunswick West. The antibiotics treated the ulcer – but things got worse before they got better. “Once you start the antibiotic treatment, it pulls the infection out,” the freelance consultant said. “There was a hole about the size of a 50¢ piece on my foot full of yellow pus. It was otherworldly looking at my foot and thinking that was on my body.” Several of her neighbours also had identical ulcers.

Advertisement

Fowler, who now has a large scar on her foot, welcomed the findings of the study. “It’s great these traps work because it is one of those things where prevention is so important,” she said. “You can’t nip it in the bud once you’ve got it. You have to go through the gruelling cycle of the infection coming out of the wound.” Director of the Western Public Health Unit in Victoria Dr Finn Romanes said there had been a 350 per cent increase in Buruli ulcer infections in the past five years across the north-west and western suburbs, where the number of cases soared from 35 in 2021 to 123 last year. “This is very significant and serious infection,” he said. “We still don’t know how it first got in, but it is really clear that it’s spreading from possums through mozzies to humans.” Romanes said high-risk suburbs grew from 12 last year to 14 this year, with Parkville and Williamstown emerging as new hotspots.

Advertisement

Related Article Science The buzz on Mosquito myths: what works to repel them and what doesn't He said the severe ulcer initially manifests as a persistent sore that will not heal, but if it is not treated with antibiotics, the bacteria slowly grows and the wound gets bigger. He urged people, particularly those living in high-risk areas, to ask their doctor for a swab test if they notice a non-healing sore. “People can suffer quite significant skin loss or deformity and sometimes even need a skin graft,” he said. He described the trial’s findings as a “moment of opportunity for public health action”.

Advertisement

“This study describes the real first urban-setting intervention that we know of which prevents transmission across a neighbourhood area,” he said. The insect traps used in the study are not yet available for purchase in Australia, but regulatory approval for their use is imminent. Romanes said authorities should explore all options, including using them for pilot schemes or free distribution of the traps to residents in high-risk zones. There were only 32 cases of the disease in 2010. In 2021, the flesh-eating ulcer spread from the Mornington and Bellarine peninsulas to inner Melbourne and, then in September 2023, a case was identified in Batemans Bay, signalling the leap of the disease to southern NSW. In 2023, infectious disease experts revealed possums would be vaccinated against the Buruli ulcer to control what they described as an astounding surge of flesh-eating disease across Victoria.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Insects The fluorescent red mozzies that could protect us from other blood-hungry biters After many years of studying Buruli ulcers, Stinear still found it remarkable that the tropical skin disease was spreading through the suburbs of Melbourne. “Thirty years ago, we didn’t really know how to detect it, treat it, or how it was spread,” he said. “Now a group of Australian researchers have answered all of those issues, and we’re moving to a bold place of well, let’s see if we can largely eliminate Buruli ulcer in Victoria.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point
text:
Advertisement

BusinessConsumer affairsEnergy ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point Nick Toscano September 6, 2026 — 12:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia has passed its tipping point in the shift away from petrol and diesel cars, Chinese auto giant BYD says, as new national sales figures show battery-electric models outsold petrol-powered vehicles last month for the first time. Australians bought 27,078 fully electric vehicles, accounting for one in four new car sales – edging out petrol vehicles (25,824) and diesel models (23,608), industry figures showed last week. When plug-in hybrids are included in the count, battery-powered cars accounted for 36 per cent of the market, while combined sales of petrol and diesel vehicles tumbled below the 50 per cent mark. Conventional hybrids made up the remainder. BYD electric vehicles unloaded at Port Melbourne. Ruby Alexander Auto executives and analysts describe the shift as a milestone for a nation that has trailed many other markets in embracing EVs.

Advertisement

“The pendulum has swung – the shift is now absolute,” said Paul Ellis, a spokesman for BYD. “It’s going to continue to increase.” Until recently, Australia had widely been considered a laggard in the uptake of electric vehicles, held back by limited model choice, high prices relative to other markets, and concerns among some consumers about whether battery-powered cars had the power and the range to cover vast distances. Related Article Electric vehicles Electric cars are taking off in Australia. Charging stations are the next challenge But electric vehicle sales have surged this year, as more Australians have sought to insulate themselves from sharply rising petrol and diesel prices due to the war between the United States and Iran cutting off global oil supplies. At the same time, an influx of lower-cost Chinese models has brought EV prices down, to be competitive with piston-powered vehicles. Ellis said consumer attitudes had shifted, reducing reluctance about EV uptake, as more Australians gained experience with electric cars.

Advertisement

“Myths have been busted,” Ellis said. “People are seeing first-hand that they are easier to drive, offer better performance, and word has been spreading.” The shift is a tailwind for efforts to slash vehicle emissions, which are polluting the atmosphere and worsening global warming. However, the pace of change poses a new challenge for governments, the auto industry and electricity companies : ensuring there are enough public chargers to cater for this year’s influx. Related Article Energy Can Australia dodge the next Iran oil shock? More than 80,000 electric vehicles had hit the road in Australia in the past three months alone, said Riz Akhtar, founder of consultancy firm Carloop. Akhtar said August 2026 sales were the “clearest sign that drivers were sick of paying high prices at the fuel pump ... going full electric and ditching petrol or diesel cars altogether.” Drivers were “making the switch faster than ever”, but fast-charging infrastructure was failing to keep up, he added. Carloop data shows NSW had 515 fast-charging sites as of last month, while Victoria had 396. “That’s going to be the biggest challenge as we expect over 30,000 more electric vehicles on Victoria’s roads, leading up to Christmas,” Akhtar said.

Advertisement

BYD’s Ellis said some prospective EV buyers were concerned about access to public charging points, not for their regular daily commute, but for longer regional road trips. “We’ve gone from ‘range anxiety’ to ‘charging anxiety’ – ‘Is there going to be a charger in Bendigo when I go there for the weekend? Will the chargers be available? Am I going to have to queue?’ “Infrastructure needs to be increased – it’s happening rapidly, but probably not quickly enough to match sales.” Last month, a major new survey of more than 42,000 members of the National Roads and Motorists Association (NRMA) found drivers of petrol and diesel vehicles were now more anxious about high fuel costs than electric vehicle owners were about funding a place to charge. NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury said the ascending sales figures showed that longstanding barriers to EV adoption were steadily falling, and 2026 would be remembered as a tipping point. “This is not a flash in the pan,” Khoury said. Toyota remained Australians’ most popular car brand in August, with 19,712 sales, down 5 per cent from a year earlier, according to the monthly sales figures from the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries and Electric Vehicle Council. In second place was BYD, up 68 per cent to 8231, followed by Tesla, up 160 per cent to 7685.

Advertisement

Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen said August’s EV sales surpassing petrol cars for the first time was a “landmark moment”. “Australians have seen through the scare campaigns and are voting with their wallets for cars that are cheaper to run, cleaner and reduce their exposure to international petrol prices shocks,” he said. title: Aussie dad's incredible garden makeover after council changes nature strip rule
text:
A simple change outside a Western Australian home has transformed a dry, weed-filled patch of grass into a colourful "wildflower meadow", with the incredible makeover bringing neighbours together.

James Mckey, 40, told Yahoo News it took him a few days and "a couple of hundred dollars" to turn the soil over and plant the new seeds, with the footpath now bordered with bright paper daisies, cornflowers and California poppies.

"I just had crushed rock out there with weeds in it. It didn't look very good so I decided to do something different," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"My thoughts have always been… you're putting the nature back in nature strip."

He said he started the journey around two and a half years ago, shortly after his local council in Toodyay — 85 kilometres north-east of Perth — changed their rules around what can and can't be planted in a verge.

One side of the path has beautiful wildflowers, while the other has a thriving veggie garden. (James Mckey)

Verge garden sparks community connection

On the other side of the footpath on the border of his property, James has planted a veggie garden complete with broccoli, cabbages, cauliflowers, silverbeet, spring onions and a variety of herbs.

"This week I had maybe 20 kilos of radishes that were all ready to be eaten," the father-of-two said.

"I pretty much stayed out there all weekend, just doing gardening, and just handing out radishes to everyone who walked past."

James, his wife and their two young children, who often help him out in the garden. (James Mckey)

In June 2024, the council modified the footpath and left James with bare soil in the nature strip. He has since grown it back. (James Mckey)

This sort of community interaction didn't exist before he planted the gardens, he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It's been a massive community-building thing," James said.

"I've met so many new people in my neighbourhood. Just being out there and working on it.

RELATED:

"And people just stop in the middle of the roundabout in traffic and yell out the window, how they love my garden," he laughed.

Admirers have even gone as far as leaving him tokens of appreciation in his letterbox, including cards, a garden tool and a painted rock.

Where to start with a verge makeover?

There's one important move all Aussie should make before embarking on a nature strip transformation.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Check your local council laws first," James advises.

With his own space, he made sure to clear the grass and weeds and turn the soil over before leaving it to rest.

Down the side of the property, James turned over the soil and planted more wildflowers. (James Mckey)

He does this so that any remaining weeds in the soil can grow enough for him to spot and pull them out.

Then it's time to sow the seeds and water regularly until they're established.

He bought his wildflower seeds from Meadowflower, and recommended their guide for creating the perfect flower bed.

title: Social algorithm opt-out locked in under legal overhaul
text:
Social media companies would have to give Australians a clear choice to opt out of algorithms under draft laws expected to be announced within weeks.

An exposure draft of a much-anticipated "digital duty of care" is expected to be released in the coming sitting fortnight as Labor steps up efforts to tackle online harm.

It would put the onus on social media companies to mitigate risk on their platforms, including actively removing illegal or harmful content.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Opt-out options for algorithms would be made mandatory, giving users the choice to take their social media feeds back to the friends-only content they once were.

The proposed changes could prevent boys from being exposed to violent and misogynistic material. (Dean Lewins/AAP PHOTOS)

Several areas are expected to be identified as off-limits to minors due to the potential for psychological harm, including content that promoted harmful body images.

Companies could face fines of up to $100 million if the laws were breached.

The changes would prevent boys from being bombarded with violent and misogynistic material, Labor's Matt Thistlethwaite told News24's Sunday Agenda program.

"Many Australian parents have said that they're concerned about their children being exposed to this material," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We think that the platforms have a responsibility to try and keep young Australian kids safe."

But the measure would fall short of the opt-in model put forward by some campaigners.

Activist Chanel Contos says the reforms do not go far enough to protect young people. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS)

Consent activist Chanel Contos recently said an algorithm opt-out was a good first step, but the measure did not go far enough to stop boys and young men being exposed to harmful content.

Instead, her organisation's Fix Our Feeds campaign calls for linear social media feeds that would only transition to algorithm-based models if users chose them.

"It would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she told the National Press Club.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said parents should have more control over what their children could see on social media.

But he was unconvinced by the latest plans from Labor, which he accused of butchering its under-16s social media ban.

More than 80 per cent of 12-to-17-year-olds were still using socials following the December 2025 crackdown, previous University of Newcastle research showed.

"The government should be focused on that because it's not working," Mr Taylor said.

"So then going off and starting on some other thing ... I think there's good reason to be sceptical about that," he said.

title: Aussie retiree finds clever solution to help the homeless feed their pets
text:
As the cost-of-living crisis makes it hard for Australians to put food on the table, one retiree is making sure pets aren't going hungry either.

Denise Clark of Melbourne knows from experience that the warmth a person feels from a dog's companionship is undeniable.

Especially for those who are unhoused, she told Yahoo News she imagines "animals are a massive part of keeping your head up".

Recognising that people who are homeless already face financial barriers to feeding and housing themselves, Denise decided earlier this year to lift at least one stressor — feeding their pets.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She did so after discovering a community food-sharing initiative where a surplus of meat and other staple grocery items were handed out for free.

By attending these initiatives, Denise said she discovered people rarely touched the meat because they weren't sure they could use it.

However, seeing people's aversion to the meat and hating seeing anything go to waste sparked her idea to turn it into meals for dogs.

With some random veggies on hand, plus oats and rice, Denise started making pet food for her own dog, who she said was a big fan of the home-cooked meals.

Do you have a cost-of-living story? Contact

Denise says she first stared making pet food just for her dog, Gypsy. Source: Denise Clark

Aussies skipping or reducing their own meals to feed pets

In her own household, Denise said she has been feeling the pinch of the cost-of-living crisis.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It's incredibly noticeable for me," she said. "Just in my general shopping at the market or the supermarkets, everything has at least doubled since Covid.

"I'm spending so much more on food."

This trend is being felt across the country as Aussies make increasingly difficult choices due to rising costs.

RELATED:

An independent national research, commissioned by the Petstock Foundation, found one in four pet owners have skipped, reduced or delayed their own meals to afford food for their pets.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Most of the 1,629 respondents in the study said pet ownership is not affordable for everyday households because of the cost of living.

Denise estimates making food for her own dog, Gypsy, once saved her about $10 to $12 a week, but believed the savings could now be closer to $15 to $20.

Denise said the cost of pet food has been skyrocketing so cooking it herself is saving her more and more money. Source: Denise Clark

Donating the meals to the Christ Church Mission Community Centre, which provides food assistance to about 900 people each week, means they can reach those doing it toughest, she said.

"People go straight for [the dog food] because they know there's so little of it, and then they go and get their food."

She now makes a batch roughly once a week, using surplus food from the community initiative as well as donations and food she buys herself when needed.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Denise's mentality is simple — good food should not go to waste when hungry people and pets could benefit from it.

"I don't want dogs suffering. I don't want human suffering, and I don't want the environment suffering."
